Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . I've got a lot of new facts now: about $81 million in reported contributions to Prop 3, which I still need to split between the Yes and No sides. The latest PPIC poll has it at 58% yes and 40% no, with the earlier September and April readings in a similar range, and a sharp partisan divide with most Democrats for it and most Republicans against.

Now I'm comparing how the poll numbers split by age and income, and I'm checking two different reports of the Democratic and Republican breakdown. I'm also noting that the CalMatters piece reports a separate poll figure for a different measure and doesn't bear on this one.

I'm checking the CalMatters income thresholds against the official figures: they list $360,000 and $721,000, while the voter guide has $371,000 and $742,000, which probably reflects a different year's inflation adjustment. I'll go with the official numbers. I'm also noting that Prop 40 is the one-time billionaire tax, Props 41 and 42 are business-backed counter-measures, and Prop 43 would require a two-thirds vote for local taxes.

I'm going to check whether Prop 41 or 42 changes personal income tax rates, since that could bring Prop 3's conflicting-measures clause into play. I also want the total campaign money behind Prop 3 and the full PPIC October report, then the neutral explainers and the Ballotpedia page.

Proposition 3
Make income taxes on higher earners permanent to fund education and healthcare
The tax, first enacted in 2012, is set to expire in 2031. Under the measure, income taxes for top earners range from 10.3% (for individual income over $360,000) to 12.3% (for individual income over $721,000), with graduated rates in between. Eighty-nine percent of the money goes to K-12 public schools and 11% goes to community colleges, with any excess going to public healthcare. The tax typically raises $5 billion to $15 billion a year — about 3% to 10% of overall K-12 spending. The California Teachers Association put this measure on the ballot.

The tax has been a vital source of revenue for schools. Supporters say if Prop. 3 fails, the loss of up to $15 billion a year for schools will likely lead to layoffs, program cuts and other reductions.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). I'm pulling together the campaign finance figures for the Yes side and the No side. The Yes committees have raised about $81 million, most of it from one education and labor committee, while the No side's main committee shows only around $5,500. That gap in money is striking, though I don't think it settles the question on its own.

The Yes side's committees are the ones with the big totals, while the No side has barely any committee money. I'm weighing that imbalance against the rest, including whether outside spending or other messaging channels could be filling the gap that the committee filings don't show. Endorsements and polling are next, with the partisan splits and the small wording discrepancy about Democratic support to sort out.

I'm checking the rest of the PPIC report for the Prop 3 breakdown, since the press release may not give the reasons behind the numbers. Next I want to verify the claims about behavioral responses to the earlier tax, the budget outlook, and how the editorial boards argued their positions.

I'm going to check whether Prop 41 or Prop 42 touch personal income tax rates, since that decides if the conflict clause in Prop 3 could come into play alongside the billionaire tax in Prop 40. Prop 40 looks like a wealth tax, so it may not qualify, but I want to confirm the wording of each before drawing a conclusion.

I'm going to check whether Prop 40 includes any language about running alongside Prop 3, since some billionaires backing Prop 3 as an alternative to the wealth tax makes that worth confirming. I also want to pull the state budget picture for 2026-27 from the LAO outlook and the enacted budget, and see how Prop 2's rainy day fund measure fits in.

I'm moving on to whether California's per-pupil spending has actually improved relative to other states and whether the extra revenue shows up in outcomes, checking the Yes side's claim against a neutral ranking. I also want to confirm that the top 2% pay about half of state income taxes, and look at how volatile the revenue is given its reliance on capital gains. Last, I'm searching for critiques of the Rauh and Kearney op-ed's claim that the state is losing more revenue from departing taxpayers than it gains.

I'm lining up the research to check next: the Prop 30 behavioral-response evidence, the Rauh and Kearney op-ed, the LAO and enacted 2026-27 budget picture, and the editorial arguments from both the Yes and No endorsers. I also want to see whether the LAO's earlier Prop 30 retrospective shows revenue above projections, since the "45% erosion" figure is contested.

The Secretary of State's contribution data is striking: about $81 million in reported support against $5,500 in opposition. Next I'll read the editorial boards on both sides, which typically lay out the strongest reasoning, along with the current budget outlook.

Endorsement: Billionaire tax is getting the attention. But Prop 3 will decide California’s future
Prop 3 would make permanent the temporary higher tax rates that voters previously approved to shore up California’s general fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, health care and other programs.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 22, 2026
California’s one-time billionaire tax is getting all the press this election cycle. But there’s another proposed tax on the wealthy this November whose fate is far more essential to the state’s finances: Proposition 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure doesn’t create a new tax or change existing ones. Instead, it cements high income tax rates on California’s biggest earners.
Those higher rates, which voters first approved in 2012 with Proposition 30 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx), were supposed to be temporary.
Prop 30 helped California survive the 2008 Great Recession by creating three new tax brackets — with a top marginal rate of 12.3% for the state’s biggest earners. (Those making more than $1 million are also taxed an additional 1%, due to a 2004 voter-approved measure to raise money for mental health services (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2004/63_11_2004.htm).)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 30 raised billions each year for the California budget’s General Fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, healthcare and other programs.
In 2016, as Prop 30’s temporary rates were set to expire, a coalition of teachers’ unions, state employee unions and healthcare advocacy groups placed Prop 55 on the ballot to keep the rates alive (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). That effort passed.
But the progressive brackets are set to expire once more in 2030. Prop 3 would make them permanent.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how it would work:
Single filers making between $73,000 and $371,000 and joint filers making between $145,000 and $743,000 currently pay (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) a personal income tax rate of 9.3%. Single filers making up to $446,000 and joint filers making up to $892,000 pay an income tax rate of 10.3%. The rate jumps to 11.3% for single filers making up to $743,000 and joint filers making up to $1.5 million. Anyone who makes more pays the max rate of 12.3%.
If voters reject Prop 3, the income tax rate would revert to 9.3% for single filers making over $73,000 and joint filers making more than $145,000. (Those earning more than $1 million would still be taxed an additional 1% from the 2004 measure.)
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) that preserving the current structure would raise between $5 billion and $15 billion annually for the General Fund. Under state spending rules, about 40% of that money would be earmarked for kindergarten through 12th-grade schools and to community colleges. The rest would be divided through the annual budget process — with a large chunk likely going to Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income residents, and some going to reserves.
Obviously, the impact of this measure failing would be enormous.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
With schools still working to recover from the pandemic and the healthcare system facing significant federal cuts under President Donald Trump, rejecting Prop 3 would be a “massive cut … at a time that we are facing massive cuts,” Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, told the editorial board.
“These revenues are not only essential to schools, but they really are now a fundamental building block of the state budget,” Karen Getman, counsel for the California Teachers Association, told us.
John Kabateck, California director of the National Federation of Independent Business, which opposes Prop 3, countered that the measure would entrench a problematic burden on small businesses. Owners who structure their businesses as “pass-throughs” (https://taxfoundation.org/blog/pass-through-businesses/) pay income taxes rather than corporate taxes — and are thus subject to the increased rates.
“Rejecting Prop 3 would be a welcome sign, frankly, for small businesses,” Kabateck told the editorial board. “Many are still crawling out of the pandemic.”
Of course, that’s also the argument that supporters of Prop 3 make.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
So, where should voters land?
In 2016, the Chronicle’s editorial board encouraged voters not to support Prop 55 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-No-on-state-Prop-55-9211163.php).
The reasoning was not that California schools and healthcare systems don’t deserve robust funding. It was that Prop 55 was a patch on a much larger problem.
California income tax revenues are inherently volatile. About half come from the top 2% of taxpayers, and therefore tend to fluctuate with the whims of the stock market.
Tying an oversized income tax to a priority as fundamental as public education is reckless. When the market tanks, as it is bound to every few years, California kids take the hardest hit.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In encouraging voters to reject Prop 55, this editorial board’s hope was that it would force state leaders to do the hard work of comprehensively reforming California’s tax system to reduce boom-and-bust cycles and instead permit stable, sustainable investment in schools, healthcare and other priorities.
That didn’t happen.
Instead, we’re getting more patches — from Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax, to Gov. Gavin Newsom and state lawmakers’ absurd decisions to raise taxes on healthcare and everyday software products (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/tax-money-state-california-22325976.php).
It’s true that voters in 2020 rejected a measure (https://calmatters.org/education/2020/11/prop-15-defeat-california-schools/) that would have modified Prop 13, the infamous 1978 measure that capped property taxes, by permitting higher taxes on large commercial properties.
With Prop 13 seemingly untouchable, income tax “seems to be the way that the voters are comfortable going” to increase revenue, Getman said.
But split roll wasn’t a solution for Prop 13, either. Voters understood that California can’t solve its issues by simply layering more taxes on top of a system that is inherently flawed.
California has the most regressive state sales taxes in the nation and an absurd income tax that hits someone making $73,000 the same as someone who makes $371,000. Even David Gamage, one of the authors of the billionaire tax, told the editorial board that he was “uncomfortable” with a top marginal income tax rate of 13.3%.
California’s tax system needs wholesale reform — by collecting stable revenue from those who can afford it and giving tax relief to the struggling middle class.
We also need greater accountability. California’s per-student spending has skyrocketed in recent years, yet academic outcomes haven’t improved commensurately (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-housing-education-reading-literacy-20288858.php). Our politicians use budget windfalls to create new programs they know they won’t be able to fund in bad times (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/03/health-care-california-budget-deficit/) — and then pass flawed patches to make up the difference.

Its judgments are made independent of the news operation , which covers the news without consideration of our editorial positions.
Prop 3 won’t resolve these problems.
And yet, in the wake of the pandemic and amid a dystopian federal climate under Trump, California also can’t afford to further reduce ongoing funds — unstable as they may be — for schools and healthcare programs. Voters should support Prop 3 to sustain funding levels but keep pressure on their politicians to work toward a fairer and more sustainable tax system. Because the one we have can and will fail.

Endorsement: No on Proposition 3, ‘temporary’ taxes should be temporary

By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 2, 2026 at 4:23 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Temporary should mean temporary. But for the government, temporary often means forever.
That’s what’s happening with Proposition 3 on the Nov. 3 ballot, titled: “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Healthcare by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes,” which, as the name suggests, seeks to lock in the state’s high income tax rates forever.
The story goes back to 2012, with Proposition 30, which imposed both a statewide sales tax increase through 2016 and an increase to top income tax rates through 2018.
Leading the push for Prop. 30 was Gov. Jerry Brown, who vowed it was only a temporary measure to help the state ride out tough budget times in the years after the Great Recession and ensure the state’s schools were reliably funded. In fact, Prop. 30 was titled, “Temporary Taxes to Fund Education.” Taken together with other voter-approved income taxes, this pushed top income tax rates to 13.3%, the highest in the nation according to the Tax Foundation, with Hawaii the runner-up at 11%.
It wasn’t long before the state’s public employee unions pounced to extend the “temporarily” increased top income tax rates over the objections of even Gov. Brown. In 2016, voters approved the extension with Proposition 55, with the taxes set to run through 2030 and expiring in 2031. As this editorial board warned at the time in opposing Prop. 55, “California will not be able to tax its way to prosperity, and imposing more taxes, particularly on those most capable of making investments here (and most capable of leaving or shifting their investments to more business-friendly states) will only reduce job opportunities and suppress economic growth.”
The argument in favor of Prop. 3 seen by voters argues that allowing Prop. 55 to expire “would give millionaires and billionaires a massive tax cut at the expense of our classrooms, clinics and communities.” But that assumes the wealthy producers will stay here, instead of getting an instant tax cut by moving to Texas or elsewhere, especially when considered in an environment in which wealth taxes are seriously being talked about.
Indeed, research published by the American Economic Association in 2024 by Joshua Rauh and Ryan J. Shyu found that the Prop. 30 tax hikes prompted many high-income earners to either leave California or lower their taxable income. Such “responses eroded 45.2 percent of state windfall tax revenues within the first year and 60.9 percent within 2 years, driven largely by the intensive margin,” Rauh and Shyu reported.

Beyond the perils of maintaining such a high tax environment, the reality is that high taxes have primarily served to paper over the fundamental budget problems of the state and the education system. As Rauh recently noted, “In California, over the 9 most recent years of data, contributions to pensions for K-12 nearly doubled as a share of educational budgets, and consumed 44% of the increase in school budgets. Prop 30/55 looks more like a tax to fund pensions than a tax to fund education.”
That’s the cold, hard reality behind any public proclamation that higher taxes are needed to help students.
Also, to reiterate, the existing Prop. 55 tax rates run through 2030, expiring in 2031. That gives Californians plenty of time, including election cycles in 2028 and 2030, to decide whether the state truly needs another extension of our sky-high income tax rates. There’s no urgent need for an extension in 2026, let alone to make the “temporary” tax hikes permanent.
R obbing future voters of their decision-making because the California Teachers Association wants to secure a revenue stream years ahead of time is unjustified.
Vote no on Prop. 3.

Both Bill Clinton and Barack Obama, the most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years, saw evaluating teacher effectiveness as a much-needed education reform. This shows Clinton walking with then-President Obama as they golfed in Maryland in 2011. (AP)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:30 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
One of the most enduring canards in public policy debates is the claim that school quality is a function of school spending. In California, this is easily disproven. Adjusted for inflation, the state spends far more per K-12 pupil now than it did in 2006-07, per (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5087) the Legislative Analyst’s Office. It’s now at an all-time high of $27,418 per student (https://www.hatchingresults.com/blog/californias-2026-27-budget).
But even as students in the Golden State are far more likely to get straight As (https://nypost.com/2026/09/13/us-news/california-high-school-gpas-soar-as-college-math-skills-decline/) than ever, their test scores have been mediocre or worse (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-k-12-test-scores/) for decades. Both red states that spend much less per-pupil (Mississippi) and blue states that spend somewhat more (Massachusetts) do significantly better jobs of preparing their high school graduates for college and life in general, according to (https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/) National Assessment of Educational Progress data.
This history is why the U-T Editorial Board has long argued that K-12 funding in the Golden State needs to be linked to the adoption of basic reforms of the sort embraced by Massachusetts in 1993 and Mississippi in 2013 — reforms that emphasized improved teaching as crucial to improved student performance. The most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years — Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — considered it common sense to coach up struggling teachers as well as struggling students.
This history is why we oppose Proposition 3 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026), placed on the ballot directly by the Legislature. It would make permanent what was first sold to voters in 2012 as a “temporary” surcharge on income taxes of wealthy residents to keep K-12 funding at adequate levels. That’s still the pitch in 2026. “Protect Local Schools Without Raising Taxes,” reads the headline on the Yes on Prop. 3 website (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQuVbaqhqGUD_FcE0tO11_EO0&gclid=CjwKCAjwwrPVBhA1EiwAv_YO-R7oAdCydz_5z0MiP0qdoGtMtcAnfk1sBvOKXl8xJj30PLr576PWPBoCmIwQAvD_BwE) — “Proposition 3 keeps the current tax rates on the wealthiest top 2% with strict accountability to ensure every dollar gets to classrooms, not Sacramento politicians.”
But “strict accountability” is not a term a rational person would associate with California’s public schools. As Stanford researchers documented (https://scale.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/GDTFII_Report_Henig.pdf), the Obama administration’s Race to the Top (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_to_the_Top) initiative that offered increased federal funding to districts that adopted reforms went nowhere in our state because of the program’s accountability edicts.
Teachers have a difficult job, and most are hardworking and eager to help their students. But in California, the unions that represent them depict attempts to measure their effectiveness as corporate attacks (https://rethinkingschools.org/articles/from-the-race-to-the-top-to-the-plunge-to-the-bottom/) on public education. In doing so, they show they value the interests of school employees over the interests of students — and society in general. Vote no on Proposition 3 to send the message that this is wrong.

Endorsement: Billionaire tax is getting the attention. But Prop 3 will decide California’s future
Prop 3 would make permanent the temporary higher tax rates that voters previously approved to shore up California’s general fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, health care and other programs.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 22, 2026
California’s one-time billionaire tax is getting all the press this election cycle. But there’s another proposed tax on the wealthy this November whose fate is far more essential to the state’s finances: Proposition 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure doesn’t create a new tax or change existing ones. Instead, it cements high income tax rates on California’s biggest earners.
Those higher rates, which voters first approved in 2012 with Proposition 30 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx), were supposed to be temporary.
Prop 30 helped California survive the 2008 Great Recession by creating three new tax brackets — with a top marginal rate of 12.3% for the state’s biggest earners. (Those making more than $1 million are also taxed an additional 1%, due to a 2004 voter-approved measure to raise money for mental health services (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2004/63_11_2004.htm).)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 30 raised billions each year for the California budget’s General Fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, healthcare and other programs.
In 2016, as Prop 30’s temporary rates were set to expire, a coalition of teachers’ unions, state employee unions and healthcare advocacy groups placed Prop 55 on the ballot to keep the rates alive (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). That effort passed.
But the progressive brackets are set to expire once more in 2030. Prop 3 would make them permanent.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how it would work:
Single filers making between $73,000 and $371,000 and joint filers making between $145,000 and $743,000 currently pay (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) a personal income tax rate of 9.3%. Single filers making up to $446,000 and joint filers making up to $892,000 pay an income tax rate of 10.3%. The rate jumps to 11.3% for single filers making up to $743,000 and joint filers making up to $1.5 million. Anyone who makes more pays the max rate of 12.3%.
If voters reject Prop 3, the income tax rate would revert to 9.3% for single filers making over $73,000 and joint filers making more than $145,000. (Those earning more than $1 million would still be taxed an additional 1% from the 2004 measure.)
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) that preserving the current structure would raise between $5 billion and $15 billion annually for the General Fund. Under state spending rules, about 40% of that money would be earmarked for kindergarten through 12th-grade schools and to community colleges. The rest would be divided through the annual budget process — with a large chunk likely going to Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income residents, and some going to reserves.
Obviously, the impact of this measure failing would be enormous.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
With schools still working to recover from the pandemic and the healthcare system facing significant federal cuts under President Donald Trump, rejecting Prop 3 would be a “massive cut … at a time that we are facing massive cuts,” Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, told the editorial board.
“These revenues are not only essential to schools, but they really are now a fundamental building block of the state budget,” Karen Getman, counsel for the California Teachers Association, told us.
John Kabateck, California director of the National Federation of Independent Business, which opposes Prop 3, countered that the measure would entrench a problematic burden on small businesses. Owners who structure their businesses as “pass-throughs” (https://taxfoundation.org/blog/pass-through-businesses/) pay income taxes rather than corporate taxes — and are thus subject to the increased rates.
“Rejecting Prop 3 would be a welcome sign, frankly, for small businesses,” Kabateck told the editorial board. “Many are still crawling out of the pandemic.”
Of course, that’s also the argument that supporters of Prop 3 make.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
So, where should voters land?
In 2016, the Chronicle’s editorial board encouraged voters not to support Prop 55 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-No-on-state-Prop-55-9211163.php).
The reasoning was not that California schools and healthcare systems don’t deserve robust funding. It was that Prop 55 was a patch on a much larger problem.
California income tax revenues are inherently volatile. About half come from the top 2% of taxpayers, and therefore tend to fluctuate with the whims of the stock market.
Tying an oversized income tax to a priority as fundamental as public education is reckless. When the market tanks, as it is bound to every few years, California kids take the hardest hit.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In encouraging voters to reject Prop 55, this editorial board’s hope was that it would force state leaders to do the hard work of comprehensively reforming California’s tax system to reduce boom-and-bust cycles and instead permit stable, sustainable investment in schools, healthcare and other priorities.
That didn’t happen.
Instead, we’re getting more patches — from Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax, to Gov. Gavin Newsom and state lawmakers’ absurd decisions to raise taxes on healthcare and everyday software products (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/tax-money-state-california-22325976.php).
It’s true that voters in 2020 rejected a measure (https://calmatters.org/education/2020/11/prop-15-defeat-california-schools/) that would have modified Prop 13, the infamous 1978 measure that capped property taxes, by permitting higher taxes on large commercial properties.
With Prop 13 seemingly untouchable, income tax “seems to be the way that the voters are comfortable going” to increase revenue, Getman said.
But split roll wasn’t a solution for Prop 13, either. Voters understood that California can’t solve its issues by simply layering more taxes on top of a system that is inherently flawed.
California has the most regressive state sales taxes in the nation and an absurd income tax that hits someone making $73,000 the same as someone who makes $371,000. Even David Gamage, one of the authors of the billionaire tax, told the editorial board that he was “uncomfortable” with a top marginal income tax rate of 13.3%.
California’s tax system needs wholesale reform — by collecting stable revenue from those who can afford it and giving tax relief to the struggling middle class.
We also need greater accountability. California’s per-student spending has skyrocketed in recent years, yet academic outcomes haven’t improved commensurately (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-housing-education-reading-literacy-20288858.php). Our politicians use budget windfalls to create new programs they know they won’t be able to fund in bad times (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/03/health-care-california-budget-deficit/) — and then pass flawed patches to make up the difference.

Prop 3 won’t resolve these problems.
And yet, in the wake of the pandemic and amid a dystopian federal climate under Trump, California also can’t afford to further reduce ongoing funds — unstable as they may be — for schools and healthcare programs. Voters should support Prop 3 to sustain funding levels but keep pressure on their politicians to work toward a fairer and more sustainable tax system. Because the one we have can and will fail.

Single filers making up to $446,000 and joint filers making up to $892,000 pay an income tax rate of 10.3%. The rate jumps to 11.3% for single filers making up to $743,000 and joint filers making up to $1.5 million. Anyone who makes more pays the max rate of 12.3%.
If voters reject Prop 3, the income tax rate would revert to 9.3% for single filers making over $73,000 and joint filers making more than $145,000. (Those earning more than $1 million would still be taxed an additional 1% from the 2004 measure.)
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) that preserving the current structure would raise between $5 billion and $15 billion annually for the General Fund. Under state spending rules, about 40% of that money would be earmarked for kindergarten through 12th-grade schools and to community colleges. The rest would be divided through the annual budget process — with a large chunk likely going to Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income residents, and some going to reserves.
Obviously, the impact of this measure failing would be enormous.

With schools still working to recover from the pandemic and the healthcare system facing significant federal cuts under President Donald Trump, rejecting Prop 3 would be a “massive cut … at a time that we are facing massive cuts,” Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, told the editorial board.
“These revenues are not only essential to schools, but they really are now a fundamental building block of the state budget,” Karen Getman, counsel for the California Teachers Association, told us.
John Kabateck, California director of the National Federation of Independent Business, which opposes Prop 3, countered that the measure would entrench a problematic burden on small businesses. Owners who structure their businesses as “pass-throughs” (https://taxfoundation.org/blog/pass-through-businesses/) pay income taxes rather than corporate taxes — and are thus subject to the increased rates.
“Rejecting Prop 3 would be a welcome sign, frankly, for small businesses,” Kabateck told the editorial board. “Many are still crawling out of the pandemic.”
Of course, that’s also the argument that supporters of Prop 3 make.

Article continues below this ad
So, where should voters land?
In 2016, the Chronicle’s editorial board encouraged voters not to support Prop 55 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-No-on-state-Prop-55-9211163.php).
The reasoning was not that California schools and healthcare systems don’t deserve robust funding. It was that Prop 55 was a patch on a much larger problem.
California income tax revenues are inherently volatile. About half come from the top 2% of taxpayers, and therefore tend to fluctuate with the whims of the stock market.
Tying an oversized income tax to a priority as fundamental as public education is reckless. When the market tanks, as it is bound to every few years, California kids take the hardest hit.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In encouraging voters to reject Prop 55, this editorial board’s hope was that it would force state leaders to do the hard work of comprehensively reforming California’s tax system to reduce boom-and-bust cycles and instead permit stable, sustainable investment in schools, healthcare and other priorities.
That didn’t happen.
Instead, we’re getting more patches — from Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax, to Gov. Gavin Newsom and state lawmakers’ absurd decisions to raise taxes on healthcare and everyday software products (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/tax-money-state-california-22325976.php).
It’s true that voters in 2020 rejected a measure (https://calmatters.org/education/2020/11/prop-15-defeat-california-schools/) that would have modified Prop 13, the infamous 1978 measure that capped property taxes, by permitting higher taxes on large commercial properties.
With Prop 13 seemingly untouchable, income tax “seems to be the way that the voters are comfortable going” to increase revenue, Getman said.
But split roll wasn’t a solution for Prop 13, either. Voters understood that California can’t solve its issues by simply layering more taxes on top of a system that is inherently flawed.
California has the most regressive state sales taxes in the nation and an absurd income tax that hits someone making $73,000 the same as someone who makes $371,000. Even David Gamage, one of the authors of the billionaire tax, told the editorial board that he was “uncomfortable” with a top marginal income tax rate of 13.3%.
California’s tax system needs wholesale reform — by collecting stable revenue from those who can afford it and giving tax relief to the struggling middle class.
We also need greater accountability. California’s per-student spending has skyrocketed in recent years, yet academic outcomes haven’t improved commensurately (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-housing-education-reading-literacy-20288858.php). Our politicians use budget windfalls to create new programs they know they won’t be able to fund in bad times (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/03/health-care-california-budget-deficit/) — and then pass flawed patches to make up the difference.

Prop 3 won’t resolve these problems.
And yet, in the wake of the pandemic and amid a dystopian federal climate under Trump, California also can’t afford to further reduce ongoing funds — unstable as they may be — for schools and healthcare programs. Voters should support Prop 3 to sustain funding levels but keep pressure on their politicians to work toward a fairer and more sustainable tax system. Because the one we have can and will fail.

Temporary should mean temporary. But for the government, temporary often means forever.
That’s what’s happening with Proposition 3 on the Nov. 3 ballot, titled: “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Healthcare by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes,” which, as the name suggests, seeks to lock in the state’s high income tax rates forever.
The story goes back to 2012, with Proposition 30, which imposed both a statewide sales tax increase through 2016 and an increase to top income tax rates through 2018.
Leading the push for Prop. 30 was Gov. Jerry Brown, who vowed it was only a temporary measure to help the state ride out tough budget times in the years after the Great Recession and ensure the state’s schools were reliably funded. In fact, Prop. 30 was titled, “Temporary Taxes to Fund Education.” Taken together with other voter-approved income taxes, this pushed top income tax rates to 13.3%, the highest in the nation according to the Tax Foundation, with Hawaii the runner-up at 11%.
It wasn’t long before the state’s public employee unions pounced to extend the “temporarily” increased top income tax rates over the objections of even Gov. Brown. In 2016, voters approved the extension with Proposition 55, with the taxes set to run through 2030 and expiring in 2031. As this editorial board warned at the time in opposing Prop. 55, “California will not be able to tax its way to prosperity, and imposing more taxes, particularly on those most capable of making investments here (and most capable of leaving or shifting their investments to more business-friendly states) will only reduce job opportunities and suppress economic growth.”

Shyu found that the Prop. 30 tax hikes prompted many high-income earners to either leave California or lower their taxable income. Leading the push for Prop. 30 was Gov. Both Bill Clinton and Barack Obama, the most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years, saw evaluating teacher effectiveness as a much-needed education reform. This shows Clinton walking with then-President Obama as they golfed in Maryland in 2011. (AP)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:30 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
One of the most enduring canards in public policy debates is the claim that school quality is a function of school spending. In California, this is easily disproven. Adjusted for inflation, the state spends far more per K-12 pupil now than it did in 2006-07, per (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5087) the Legislative Analyst’s Office. It’s now at an all-time high of $27,418 per student (https://www.hatchingresults.com/blog/californias-2026-27-budget).
But even as students in the Golden State are far more likely to get straight As (https://nypost.com/2026/09/13/us-news/california-high-school-gpas-soar-as-college-math-skills-decline/) than ever, their test scores have been mediocre or worse (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-k-12-test-scores/) for decades. Both red states that spend much less per-pupil (Mississippi) and blue states that spend somewhat more (Massachusetts) do significantly better jobs of preparing their high school graduates for college and life in general, according to (https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/) National Assessment of Educational Progress data.
This history is why the U-T Editorial Board has long argued that K-12 funding in the Golden State needs to be linked to the adoption of basic reforms of the sort embraced by Massachusetts in 1993 and Mississippi in 2013 — reforms that emphasized improved teaching as crucial to improved student performance. The most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years — Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — considered it common sense to coach up struggling teachers as well as struggling students.
This history is why we oppose Proposition 3 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026), placed on the ballot directly by the Legislature. It would make permanent what was first sold to voters in 2012 as a “temporary” surcharge on income taxes of wealthy residents to keep K-12 funding at adequate levels. That’s still the pitch in 2026. “Protect Local Schools Without Raising Taxes,” reads the headline on the Yes on Prop. 3 website (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQuVbaqhqGUD_FcE0tO11_EO0&gclid=CjwKCAjwwrPVBhA1EiwAv_YO-R7oAdCydz_5z0MiP0qdoGtMtcAnfk1sBvOKXl8xJj30PLr576PWPBoCmIwQAvD_BwE) — “Proposition 3 keeps the current tax rates on the wealthiest top 2% with strict accountability to ensure every dollar gets to classrooms, not Sacramento politicians.”
But “strict accountability” is not a term a rational person would associate with California’s public schools. As Stanford researchers documented (https://scale.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/GDTFII_Report_Henig.pdf), the Obama administration’s Race to the Top (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_to_the_Top) initiative that offered increased federal funding to districts that adopted reforms went nowhere in our state because of the program’s accountability edicts.
Teachers have a difficult job, and most are hardworking and eager to help their students. But in California, the unions that represent them depict attempts to measure their effectiveness as corporate attacks (https://rethinkingschools.org/articles/from-the-race-to-the-top-to-the-plunge-to-the-bottom/) on public education. In doing so, they show they value the interests of school employees over the interests of students — and society in general. Vote no on Proposition 3 to send the message that this is wrong.

Both Bill Clinton and Barack Obama, the most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years, saw evaluating teacher effectiveness as a much-needed education reform. This shows Clinton walking with then-President Obama as they golfed in Maryland in 2011. (AP)
By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:30 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
One of the most enduring canards in public policy debates is the claim that school quality is a function of school spending. In California, this is easily disproven. Adjusted for inflation, the state spends far more per K-12 pupil now than it did in 2006-07, per (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5087) the Legislative Analyst’s Office. It’s now at an all-time high of $27,418 per student (https://www.hatchingresults.com/blog/californias-2026-27-budget).
But even as students in the Golden State are far more likely to get straight As (https://nypost.com/2026/09/13/us-news/california-high-school-gpas-soar-as-college-math-skills-decline/) than ever, their test scores have been mediocre or worse (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-k-12-test-scores/) for decades. Both red states that spend much less per-pupil (Mississippi) and blue states that spend somewhat more (Massachusetts) do significantly better jobs of preparing their high school graduates for college and life in general, according to (https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/) National Assessment of Educational Progress data.
This history is why the U-T Editorial Board has long argued that K-12 funding in the Golden State needs to be linked to the adoption of basic reforms of the sort embraced by Massachusetts in 1993 and Mississippi in 2013 — reforms that emphasized improved teaching as crucial to improved student performance. The most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years — Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — considered it common sense to coach up struggling teachers as well as struggling students.
This history is why we oppose Proposition 3 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026), placed on the ballot directly by the Legislature. It would make permanent what was first sold to voters in 2012 as a “temporary” surcharge on income taxes of wealthy residents to keep K-12 funding at adequate levels. That’s still the pitch in 2026. “Protect Local Schools Without Raising Taxes,” reads the headline on the Yes on Prop. 3 website (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQuVbaqhqGUD_FcE0tO11_EO0&gclid=CjwKCAjwwrPVBhA1EiwAv_YO-R7oAdCydz_5z0MiP0qdoGtMtcAnfk1sBvOKXl8xJj30PLr576PWPBoCmIwQAvD_BwE) — “Proposition 3 keeps the current tax rates on the wealthiest top 2% with strict accountability to ensure every dollar gets to classrooms, not Sacramento politicians.”
But “strict accountability” is not a term a rational person would associate with California’s public schools. As Stanford researchers documented (https://scale.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/GDTFII_Report_Henig.pdf), the Obama administration’s Race to the Top (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_to_the_Top) initiative that offered increased federal funding to districts that adopted reforms went nowhere in our state because of the program’s accountability edicts.
Teachers have a difficult job, and most are hardworking and eager to help their students. But in California, the unions that represent them depict attempts to measure their effectiveness as corporate attacks (https://rethinkingschools.org/articles/from-the-race-to-the-top-to-the-plunge-to-the-bottom/) on public education. In doing so, they show they value the interests of school employees over the interests of students — and society in general. Vote no on Proposition 3 to send the message that this is wrong.

I'm pulling together the campaign finance figures for the Yes side and the No side. The Yes committees have raised about $81 million, most of it from one education and labor committee, while the No side's main committee shows only around $5,500. That gap in money is striking, though I don't think it settles the question on its own.

The Yes side's committees are the ones with the big totals, while the No side has barely any committee money. I'm weighing that imbalance against the rest, including whether outside spending or other messaging channels could be filling the gap that the committee filings don't show. Endorsements and polling are next, with the partisan splits and the small wording discrepancy about Democratic support to sort out.

I'm checking the rest of the PPIC report for the Prop 3 breakdown, since the press release may not give the reasons behind the numbers. Next I want to verify the claims about behavioral responses to the earlier tax, the budget outlook, and how the editorial boards argued their positions.

I'm going to check whether Prop 41 or Prop 42 touch personal income tax rates, since that decides if the conflict clause in Prop 3 could come into play alongside the billionaire tax in Prop 40. Prop 40 looks like a wealth tax, so it may not qualify, but I want to confirm the wording of each before drawing a conclusion.

I'm going to check whether Prop 40 includes any language about running alongside Prop 3, since some billionaires backing Prop 3 as an alternative to the wealth tax makes that worth confirming. I also want to pull the state budget picture for 2026-27 from the LAO outlook and the enacted budget, and see how Prop 2's rainy day fund measure fits in.

I'm moving on to whether California's per-pupil spending has actually improved relative to other states and whether the extra revenue shows up in outcomes, checking the Yes side's claim against a neutral ranking. I also want to confirm that the top 2% pay about half of state income taxes, and look at how volatile the revenue is given its reliance on capital gains. Last, I'm searching for critiques of the Rauh and Kearney op-ed's claim that the state is losing more revenue from departing taxpayers than it gains.

I'm lining up the research to check next: the Prop 30 behavioral-response evidence, the Rauh and Kearney op-ed, the LAO and enacted 2026-27 budget picture, and the editorial arguments from both the Yes and No endorsers. I also want to see whether the LAO's earlier Prop 30 retrospective shows revenue above projections, since the "45% erosion" figure is contested.
