Endorsement: Billionaire tax is getting the attention. But Prop 3 will decide California’s future
Prop 3 would make permanent the temporary higher tax rates that voters previously approved to shore up California’s general fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, health care and other programs.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 22, 2026
California’s one-time billionaire tax is getting all the press this election cycle. But there’s another proposed tax on the wealthy this November whose fate is far more essential to the state’s finances: Proposition 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure doesn’t create a new tax or change existing ones. Instead, it cements high income tax rates on California’s biggest earners.
Those higher rates, which voters first approved in 2012 with Proposition 30 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx), were supposed to be temporary.
Prop 30 helped California survive the 2008 Great Recession by creating three new tax brackets — with a top marginal rate of 12.3% for the state’s biggest earners. (Those making more than $1 million are also taxed an additional 1%, due to a 2004 voter-approved measure to raise money for mental health services (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2004/63_11_2004.htm).)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 30 raised billions each year for the California budget’s General Fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, healthcare and other programs.
In 2016, as Prop 30’s temporary rates were set to expire, a coalition of teachers’ unions, state employee unions and healthcare advocacy groups placed Prop 55 on the ballot to keep the rates alive (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). That effort passed.
But the progressive brackets are set to expire once more in 2030. Prop 3 would make them permanent.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how it would work:
Single filers making between $73,000 and $371,000 and joint filers making between $145,000 and $743,000 currently pay (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) a personal income tax rate of 9.3%. Single filers making up to $446,000 and joint filers making up to $892,000 pay an income tax rate of 10.3%. The rate jumps to 11.3% for single filers making up to $743,000 and joint filers making up to $1.5 million. Anyone who makes more pays the max rate of 12.3%.
If voters reject Prop 3, the income tax rate would revert to 9.3% for single filers making over $73,000 and joint filers making more than $145,000. (Those earning more than $1 million would still be taxed an additional 1% from the 2004 measure.)
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) that preserving the current structure would raise between $5 billion and $15 billion annually for the General Fund. Under state spending rules, about 40% of that money would be earmarked for kindergarten through 12th-grade schools and to community colleges. The rest would be divided through the annual budget process — with a large chunk likely going to Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income residents, and some going to reserves.
Obviously, the impact of this measure failing would be enormous.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
With schools still working to recover from the pandemic and the healthcare system facing significant federal cuts under President Donald Trump, rejecting Prop 3 would be a “massive cut … at a time that we are facing massive cuts,” Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, told the editorial board.
“These revenues are not only essential to schools, but they really are now a fundamental building block of the state budget,” Karen Getman, counsel for the California Teachers Association, told us.
John Kabateck, California director of the National Federation of Independent Business, which opposes Prop 3, countered that the measure would entrench a problematic burden on small businesses. Owners who structure their businesses as “pass-throughs” (https://taxfoundation.org/blog/pass-through-businesses/) pay income taxes rather than corporate taxes — and are thus subject to the increased rates.
“Rejecting Prop 3 would be a welcome sign, frankly, for small businesses,” Kabateck told the editorial board. “Many are still crawling out of the pandemic.”
Of course, that’s also the argument that supporters of Prop 3 make.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
So, where should voters land?
In 2016, the Chronicle’s editorial board encouraged voters not to support Prop 55 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-No-on-state-Prop-55-9211163.php).
The reasoning was not that California schools and healthcare systems don’t deserve robust funding. It was that Prop 55 was a patch on a much larger problem.
California income tax revenues are inherently volatile. About half come from the top 2% of taxpayers, and therefore tend to fluctuate with the whims of the stock market.
Tying an oversized income tax to a priority as fundamental as public education is reckless. When the market tanks, as it is bound to every few years, California kids take the hardest hit.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In encouraging voters to reject Prop 55, this editorial board’s hope was that it would force state leaders to do the hard work of comprehensively reforming California’s tax system to reduce boom-and-bust cycles and instead permit stable, sustainable investment in schools, healthcare and other priorities.
That didn’t happen.
Instead, we’re getting more patches — from Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax, to Gov. Gavin Newsom and state lawmakers’ absurd decisions to raise taxes on healthcare and everyday software products (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/tax-money-state-california-22325976.php).
It’s true that voters in 2020 rejected a measure (https://calmatters.org/education/2020/11/prop-15-defeat-california-schools/) that would have modified Prop 13, the infamous 1978 measure that capped property taxes, by permitting higher taxes on large commercial properties.
With Prop 13 seemingly untouchable, income tax “seems to be the way that the voters are comfortable going” to increase revenue, Getman said.
But split roll wasn’t a solution for Prop 13, either. Voters understood that California can’t solve its issues by simply layering more taxes on top of a system that is inherently flawed.
California has the most regressive state sales taxes in the nation and an absurd income tax that hits someone making $73,000 the same as someone who makes $371,000. Even David Gamage, one of the authors of the billionaire tax, told the editorial board that he was “uncomfortable” with a top marginal income tax rate of 13.3%.
California’s tax system needs wholesale reform — by collecting stable revenue from those who can afford it and giving tax relief to the struggling middle class.
We also need greater accountability. California’s per-student spending has skyrocketed in recent years, yet academic outcomes haven’t improved commensurately (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-housing-education-reading-literacy-20288858.php). Our politicians use budget windfalls to create new programs they know they won’t be able to fund in bad times (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/03/health-care-california-budget-deficit/) — and then pass flawed patches to make up the difference.

Prop 3 won’t resolve these problems.
And yet, in the wake of the pandemic and amid a dystopian federal climate under Trump, California also can’t afford to further reduce ongoing funds — unstable as they may be — for schools and healthcare programs. Voters should support Prop 3 to sustain funding levels but keep pressure on their politicians to work toward a fairer and more sustainable tax system. Because the one we have can and will fail.

Endorsement: No on Proposition 3, ‘temporary’ taxes should be temporary

By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 2, 2026 at 4:23 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Temporary should mean temporary. But for the government, temporary often means forever.
That’s what’s happening with Proposition 3 on the Nov. 3 ballot, titled: “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Healthcare by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes,” which, as the name suggests, seeks to lock in the state’s high income tax rates forever.
The story goes back to 2012, with Proposition 30, which imposed both a statewide sales tax increase through 2016 and an increase to top income tax rates through 2018.
Leading the push for Prop. 30 was Gov. Jerry Brown, who vowed it was only a temporary measure to help the state ride out tough budget times in the years after the Great Recession and ensure the state’s schools were reliably funded. In fact, Prop. 30 was titled, “Temporary Taxes to Fund Education.” Taken together with other voter-approved income taxes, this pushed top income tax rates to 13.3%, the highest in the nation according to the Tax Foundation, with Hawaii the runner-up at 11%.
It wasn’t long before the state’s public employee unions pounced to extend the “temporarily” increased top income tax rates over the objections of even Gov. Brown. In 2016, voters approved the extension with Proposition 55, with the taxes set to run through 2030 and expiring in 2031. As this editorial board warned at the time in opposing Prop. 55, “California will not be able to tax its way to prosperity, and imposing more taxes, particularly on those most capable of making investments here (and most capable of leaving or shifting their investments to more business-friendly states) will only reduce job opportunities and suppress economic growth.”
The argument in favor of Prop. 3 seen by voters argues that allowing Prop. 55 to expire “would give millionaires and billionaires a massive tax cut at the expense of our classrooms, clinics and communities.” But that assumes the wealthy producers will stay here, instead of getting an instant tax cut by moving to Texas or elsewhere, especially when considered in an environment in which wealth taxes are seriously being talked about.
Indeed, research published by the American Economic Association in 2024 by Joshua Rauh and Ryan J. Shyu found that the Prop. 30 tax hikes prompted many high-income earners to either leave California or lower their taxable income. Such “responses eroded 45.2 percent of state windfall tax revenues within the first year and 60.9 percent within 2 years, driven largely by the intensive margin,” Rauh and Shyu reported.

Beyond the perils of maintaining such a high tax environment, the reality is that high taxes have primarily served to paper over the fundamental budget problems of the state and the education system. As Rauh recently noted, “In California, over the 9 most recent years of data, contributions to pensions for K-12 nearly doubled as a share of educational budgets, and consumed 44% of the increase in school budgets. Prop 30/55 looks more like a tax to fund pensions than a tax to fund education.”
That’s the cold, hard reality behind any public proclamation that higher taxes are needed to help students.
Also, to reiterate, the existing Prop. 55 tax rates run through 2030, expiring in 2031. That gives Californians plenty of time, including election cycles in 2028 and 2030, to decide whether the state truly needs another extension of our sky-high income tax rates. There’s no urgent need for an extension in 2026, let alone to make the “temporary” tax hikes permanent.
R obbing future voters of their decision-making because the California Teachers Association wants to secure a revenue stream years ahead of time is unjustified.
Vote no on Prop. 3.

By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:30 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
One of the most enduring canards in public policy debates is the claim that school quality is a function of school spending. In California, this is easily disproven. Adjusted for inflation, the state spends far more per K-12 pupil now than it did in 2006-07, per (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5087) the Legislative Analyst’s Office. It’s now at an all-time high of $27,418 per student (https://www.hatchingresults.com/blog/californias-2026-27-budget).
But even as students in the Golden State are far more likely to get straight As (https://nypost.com/2026/09/13/us-news/california-high-school-gpas-soar-as-college-math-skills-decline/) than ever, their test scores have been mediocre or worse (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-k-12-test-scores/) for decades. Both red states that spend much less per-pupil (Mississippi) and blue states that spend somewhat more (Massachusetts) do significantly better jobs of preparing their high school graduates for college and life in general, according to (https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/) National Assessment of Educational Progress data.
This history is why the U-T Editorial Board has long argued that K-12 funding in the Golden State needs to be linked to the adoption of basic reforms of the sort embraced by Massachusetts in 1993 and Mississippi in 2013 — reforms that emphasized improved teaching as crucial to improved student performance. The most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years — Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — considered it common sense to coach up struggling teachers as well as struggling students.
This history is why we oppose Proposition 3 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026), placed on the ballot directly by the Legislature. It would make permanent what was first sold to voters in 2012 as a “temporary” surcharge on income taxes of wealthy residents to keep K-12 funding at adequate levels. That’s still the pitch in 2026. “Protect Local Schools Without Raising Taxes,” reads the headline on the Yes on Prop. 3 website (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQuVbaqhqGUD_FcE0tO11_EO0&gclid=CjwKCAjwwrPVBhA1EiwAv_YO-R7oAdCydz_5z0MiP0qdoGtMtcAnfk1sBvOKXl8xJj30PLr576PWPBoCmIwQAvD_BwE) — “Proposition 3 keeps the current tax rates on the wealthiest top 2% with strict accountability to ensure every dollar gets to classrooms, not Sacramento politicians.”
But “strict accountability” is not a term a rational person would associate with California’s public schools. As Stanford researchers documented (https://scale.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/GDTFII_Report_Henig.pdf), the Obama administration’s Race to the Top (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_to_the_Top) initiative that offered increased federal funding to districts that adopted reforms went nowhere in our state because of the program’s accountability edicts.
Teachers have a difficult job, and most are hardworking and eager to help their students. But in California, the unions that represent them depict attempts to measure their effectiveness as corporate attacks (https://rethinkingschools.org/articles/from-the-race-to-the-top-to-the-plunge-to-the-bottom/) on public education. In doing so, they show they value the interests of school employees over the interests of students — and society in general. Vote no on Proposition 3 to send the message that this is wrong.

I'm checking whether the paper's finding that high earners mostly responded by shifting when they realized income, rather than leaving, holds up, since timing effects could mean the erosion isn't permanent. I also want to confirm the LAO's read on Prop 30 revenue against the earlier estimates, and find critiques of the Rauh and Shyu study.

I'm checking the state budget picture next, including the LAO's fiscal outlook and how the No side's claim about a swing from surplus to deficit holds up. I also want to see where the governor stands on Prop 3, since the SF Chronicle piece references recent tax decisions in Sacramento.

## Abstract
Drawing on the universe of California income tax filings and the variation imposed by a 2012 tax increase of up to 3 percentage points for high-income households, we present new findings about the effects of personal income taxation on household location choice and pre-tax income.
First, over and above baseline rates of taxpayer departure from California, an additional 0.8% of the California residential tax filing base whose 2012 income would have been in the new top tax bracket moved out from full-year residency of California in 2013, mostly to states with zero income tax.
Second, to identify the impact of the California tax policy shift on the pre-tax earnings of high-income California residents, we use as a control group high-earning out-of-state taxpayers who persistently file as California non-residents.
Using a differences-in-differences strategy paired with propensity score matching, we estimate an intensive margin elasticity of 2013 income with respect to the marginal net-of-tax rate of 2.5 to 3.3.
Among top-bracket California taxpayers, outward migration and behavioral responses by stayers together eroded 45.2% of the windfall tax revenues from the reform.

In its first issue of 2024, the *American Economic Journal: Economic Policy* published three academic articles addressing a complex relationship between state taxes and individual decisions on where to live and work in the United States.
...
The second article, “Behavioral Responses to State Income Taxation of High Earners: Evidence from California,” by Joshua Rauh and Ryan Shyu, focuses on California’s Proposition 30, which significantly increased marginal tax rates for high-earning individuals in the state in 2012.
The authors use administrative microdata and modern methods of causal analysis to demonstrate that high earners were indeed very sensitive to Proposition 30.
In response to the 3-percentage-point increase in the top marginal state income tax rate, which reached 13.3 percent in 2012, high earners reported $321,000-$436,000 less in taxable income during 2012-2014—about 10 percent of their baseline income of $4.15 million.
The likely reasons were the reduction in labor supply, shifting income-generating activities to other countries, or other forms of tax avoidance.
Rauh and Shyu also discuss the implications of the SALT cap deduction introduced as part of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, arguing that this cap increased the incentives for high-income individuals to consider moving to lower-tax states even more than Proposition 30 did.

## Abstract
Drawing on the universe of California income tax filings and the variation imposed by a 2012 tax increase of up to 3 percentage points for high-income households, we present new findings about the effects of personal income taxation on household location choice and pre-tax income.
First, over and above baseline rates of taxpayer departure from California, an additional 0.8% of the California residential tax filing base whose 2012 income would have been in the new top tax bracket moved out from full-year residency of California in 2013, mostly to states with zero income tax.
Second, to identify the impact of the California tax policy shift on the pre-tax earnings of high-income California residents, we use as a control group high-earning out-of-state taxpayers who persistently file as California non-residents.
Using a differences-in-differences strategy paired with propensity score matching, we estimate an intensive margin elasticity of 2013 income with respect to the marginal net-of-tax rate of 2.5 to 3.3.
Among top-bracket California taxpayers, outward migration and behavioral responses by stayers together eroded 45.2% of the windfall tax revenues from the reform.

The Budget Act of 2026 meets the Foundation for the Future framework and provides a solid, responsible budget for the people of California.
The budget builds record reserves, protects core programs and delays certain program cuts, makes targeted new investments, and includes difficult spending and revenue decisions to balance the budget through 2027-28 and cut the long-term structural deficit in half.
The Budget Act of 2026 provides $351.7 billion in total expenditures in 2026-27, including $251.5 billion from the General Fund, and contains record total reserves of $35.2 billion, including:
$4.5 billion in the Regular Reserve (Special Fund for Economic Uncertainties).

#### Abstract
Using administrative data, we analyze the response to Proposition 30, a 2012 measure that increased California marginal tax rates by up to 3 percentage points for high-income households.
Relative to baseline departure rates, an additional 0.8 percent of the residential tax base that landed in the top bracket left California in 2013.
Using matched out-of-state taxpayers as controls reveals an income elasticity with respect to the marginal net-of-tax rate of 2.5–3.2 for high earners who stayed.

The new issue of the *American Economic Journal: Economic Policy* is out and it contains a study by economists Joshua Rauh and Ryan Shyu titled “Behavioral Responses to State Income Taxation of High Earners: Evidence from California.”

They also found that these departures and other responses to increased taxes eliminated 45.2% of the revenue the state expected to get from high earners.

## Abstract
Drawing on the universe of California income tax filings and the variation imposed by a 2012 tax increase of up to 3 percentage points for high-income households, we present new findings about the effects of personal income taxation on household location choice and pre-tax income.
First, over and above baseline rates of taxpayer departure from California, an additional 0.8% of the California residential tax filing base whose 2012 income would have been in the new top tax bracket moved out from full-year residency of California in 2013, mostly to states with zero income tax.
Second, to identify the impact of the California tax policy shift on the pre-tax earnings of high-income California residents, we use as a control group high-earning out-of-state taxpayers who persistently file as California non-residents.
Using a differences-in-differences strategy paired with propensity score matching, we estimate an intensive margin elasticity of 2013 income with respect to the marginal net-of-tax rate of 2.5 to 3.3.
Among top-bracket California taxpayers, outward migration and behavioral responses by stayers together eroded 45.2% of the windfall tax revenues from the reform.

# Taxes and Migration: New Evidence from Academic Research
In its first issue of 2024, the *American Economic Journal: Economic Policy* published three academic articles addressing a complex relationship between state taxes and individual decisions on where to live and work in the United States.
...
The second article, “Behavioral Responses to State Income Taxation of High Earners: Evidence from California,” by Joshua Rauh and Ryan Shyu, focuses on California’s Proposition 30, which significantly increased marginal tax rates for high-earning individuals in the state in 2012.
The authors use administrative microdata and modern methods of causal analysis to demonstrate that high earners were indeed very sensitive to Proposition 30.
In response to the 3-percentage-point increase in the top marginal state income tax rate, which reached 13.3 percent in 2012, high earners reported $321,000-$436,000 less in taxable income during 2012-2014—about 10 percent of their baseline income of $4.15 million.
The likely reasons were the reduction in labor supply, shifting income-generating activities to other countries, or other forms of tax avoidance.
Rauh and Shyu also discuss the implications of the SALT cap deduction introduced as part of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, arguing that this cap increased the incentives for high-income individuals to consider moving to lower-tax states even more than Proposition 30 did.

California’s richest are doing great.
Over the last four decades, while the bottom four-fifths of households have seen their real incomes decline, the top 1% have seen their real incomes grow two and half times (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). This upper stratum now earns in a week what the middle fifth of Californians make in a year.
Proposition 3 asks the Californians truly living the California dream to keep paying their fair share. No more. No less.
Vote for Proposition 3.

In 2012, voters approved Proposition 30 to temporarily increase marginal rates on the top 2% of earners; and in 2016, they approved Proposition 55 to extend these same rates until 2030.
Now on the Nov. 3 ballot, Proposition 3 would keep these existing rates in place permanently after 2030.
The measure only applies to individuals whose incomes exceed $371,000 or joint filers whose incomes exceed $743,000. (The median full-time worker in California earns $65,000 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/who-are-californias-workers/). The median family’s income is $100,000 (https://data.census.gov/profile/California?g=040XX00US06).)
If Proposition 3 fails, the state’s General Fund would lose between $5 billion and $15 billion per year, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office projections (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Around 40% of those lost revenues would have gone to California’s public schools and colleges; the remainder would fund other state services, including healthcare, and the state’s rainy day reserve fund.
However, should it fail, the richest Californians would get a large windfall, the vast majority of which would flow to the top 1%.
Extremely disingenuous
The campaign against Proposition 3, sponsored by the California Taxpayers Association, ranges from merely misleading to downright scurrilous.
The main tactic used by the California Taxpayers Association, whose board of directors includes heads of the world’s biggest businesses, is to hide behind small businesses. Proposition 3, they argue, will hurt small business owners because “many” operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships and S Corps, and they report their business earnings on personal income taxes.
That might sound convincing until you look at Census and Franchise Tax Board data.
It turns out, the average revenue for the state’s nonemployer businesses — be they C corps, S corps, individual proprietorships, etc. — is less than $65,000. In other words, the vast majority of the state’s smallest businesses don’t make anywhere near enough to have to pay these higher rates. Invoking them, as opponents do, is absurd.
But what about prices. Will Proposition 3 raise prices and thus inflate inflation?
Opponents claim that small businesses will just pass the costs of this tax onto consumers. That might sound logical until you realize that Proposition 3 won’t raise taxes. It preserves existing ones.
Why would businesses suddenly raise prices because voters decided to maintain tax rates in place for the last 13 years?
They wouldn’t.
Perhaps the most dishonest attack on this progressive tax is that it will push the state’s wealthy out of the state and discourage investment.
Evidence from the last decade completely throws cold water on those fears of capital flight.
Millionaire factory
California’s share of the country’s millionaires and billionaires increased during the last decade (https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/CAwealthtax.pdf), as UC Berkeley’s Econometrics Lab found.
And Franchise Tax Board data show the same: The number of tax filers subject to the top tax rates more than doubled between 2013, when these higher rates went into effect, and 2024.
No serious economic analyst could look at the last decade and a half and call it an era of disinvestment or economic malaise in California. After all, this exact period saw California lead the planet in global investment, innovation and wealth creation. Our big companies — Apple, Alphabet, Meta, Netflix and Nvidia — became the biggest. And our early-stage startups, led by high-skilled talent, attracted historic levels of capital and then became globally dominant business behemoths, like Uber and Airbnb.
And that investment hasn’t stopped, just because the top 2% has been paying two or three percentage points more on their income taxes.
California’s startups attracted $366 billion from venture capitalists in the first six months of this year. (https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/californias-ai-dominance-fuels-366-billion-venture-capital-bonanza-820e9bde) Not only is that double its previous record but it’s three times the amount invested in the other 49 states combined. The total volume of capital invested in this one sector of the state in just half a year exceeds the annual economies of 25 states.
The fearmongering about these progressive taxes defies logic.
New urgency
Over the last year, the reason for keeping these rates in place has become even more urgent.
As a result of a vindictive Republican Congress and president, California will lose billions in federal funds. H.R. 1, or the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, is shifting the costs of maintaining our safety net back onto this state. California’s counties, which maintain the safety net, expect to lose as much as $9.5 billion per year (https://www.counties.org/hr1/https:/www.counties.org/hr1/).
Already, local governments, including Santa Clara County, are resorting to regressive sales taxes to prop up services once sustained with progressive federal taxes. Bay Area hospitals are seeing the number of uninsured in their emergency rooms double, as this news organization has documented.
Rejecting Proposition 3 would compound that problem, depriving the state of billions while handing a giant windfall to the Californians who need it least.
Proposition 40 was a different beast. (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/21/endorsement-reject-california-ballot-propositions-40-41-42-billionaires-tax-ai-inequality/) We opposed it. It was retroactive. It taxed wealth. It was new, and it does risk creating capital flight.
But Proposition 3 has none of those defects.
Vote yes.

California’s richest are doing great.
Over the last four decades, while the bottom four-fifths of households have seen their real incomes decline, the top 1% have seen their real incomes grow two and half times (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). This upper stratum now earns in a week what the middle fifth of Californians make in a year.
Proposition 3 asks the Californians truly living the California dream to keep paying their fair share. No more. No less.
Vote for Proposition 3.

In 2012, voters approved Proposition 30 to temporarily increase marginal rates on the top 2% of earners; and in 2016, they approved Proposition 55 to extend these same rates until 2030.
Now on the Nov. 3 ballot, Proposition 3 would keep these existing rates in place permanently after 2030.
The measure only applies to individuals whose incomes exceed $371,000 or joint filers whose incomes exceed $743,000. (The median full-time worker in California earns $65,000 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/who-are-californias-workers/). The median family’s income is $100,000 (https://data.census.gov/profile/California?g=040XX00US06).)
If Proposition 3 fails, the state’s General Fund would lose between $5 billion and $15 billion per year, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office projections (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Around 40% of those lost revenues would have gone to California’s public schools and colleges; the remainder would fund other state services, including healthcare, and the state’s rainy day reserve fund.
However, should it fail, the richest Californians would get a large windfall, the vast majority of which would flow to the top 1%.
Extremely disingenuous
The campaign against Proposition 3, sponsored by the California Taxpayers Association, ranges from merely misleading to downright scurrilous.
The main tactic used by the California Taxpayers Association, whose board of directors includes heads of the world’s biggest businesses, is to hide behind small businesses. Proposition 3, they argue, will hurt small business owners because “many” operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships and S Corps, and they report their business earnings on personal income taxes.
That might sound convincing until you look at Census and Franchise Tax Board data.
It turns out, the average revenue for the state’s nonemployer businesses — be they C corps, S corps, individual proprietorships, etc. — is less than $65,000. In other words, the vast majority of the state’s smallest businesses don’t make anywhere near enough to have to pay these higher rates. Invoking them, as opponents do, is absurd.
But what about prices. Will Proposition 3 raise prices and thus inflate inflation?
Opponents claim that small businesses will just pass the costs of this tax onto consumers. That might sound logical until you realize that Proposition 3 won’t raise taxes. It preserves existing ones.
Why would businesses suddenly raise prices because voters decided to maintain tax rates in place for the last 13 years?
They wouldn’t.
Perhaps the most dishonest attack on this progressive tax is that it will push the state’s wealthy out of the state and discourage investment.
Evidence from the last decade completely throws cold water on those fears of capital flight.
Millionaire factory
California’s share of the country’s millionaires and billionaires increased during the last decade (https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/CAwealthtax.pdf), as UC Berkeley’s Econometrics Lab found.
And Franchise Tax Board data show the same: The number of tax filers subject to the top tax rates more than doubled between 2013, when these higher rates went into effect, and 2024.
No serious economic analyst could look at the last decade and a half and call it an era of disinvestment or economic malaise in California. After all, this exact period saw California lead the planet in global investment, innovation and wealth creation. Our big companies — Apple, Alphabet, Meta, Netflix and Nvidia — became the biggest. And our early-stage startups, led by high-skilled talent, attracted historic levels of capital and then became globally dominant business behemoths, like Uber and Airbnb.
And that investment hasn’t stopped, just because the top 2% has been paying two or three percentage points more on their income taxes.
California’s startups attracted $366 billion from venture capitalists in the first six months of this year. (https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/californias-ai-dominance-fuels-366-billion-venture-capital-bonanza-820e9bde) Not only is that double its previous record but it’s three times the amount invested in the other 49 states combined. The total volume of capital invested in this one sector of the state in just half a year exceeds the annual economies of 25 states.
The fearmongering about these progressive taxes defies logic.
New urgency
Over the last year, the reason for keeping these rates in place has become even more urgent.
As a result of a vindictive Republican Congress and president, California will lose billions in federal funds. H.R. 1, or the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, is shifting the costs of maintaining our safety net back onto this state. California’s counties, which maintain the safety net, expect to lose as much as $9.5 billion per year (https://www.counties.org/hr1/https:/www.counties.org/hr1/).
Already, local governments, including Santa Clara County, are resorting to regressive sales taxes to prop up services once sustained with progressive federal taxes. Bay Area hospitals are seeing the number of uninsured in their emergency rooms double, as this news organization has documented.
Rejecting Proposition 3 would compound that problem, depriving the state of billions while handing a giant windfall to the Californians who need it least.
Proposition 40 was a different beast. (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/21/endorsement-reject-california-ballot-propositions-40-41-42-billionaires-tax-ai-inequality/) We opposed it. It was retroactive. It taxed wealth. It was new, and it does risk creating capital flight.
But Proposition 3 has none of those defects.
Vote yes.

California’s richest are doing great.
Over the last four decades, while the bottom four-fifths of households have seen their real incomes decline, the top 1% have seen their real incomes grow two and half times (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). This upper stratum now earns in a week what the middle fifth of Californians make in a year.
Proposition 3 asks the Californians truly living the California dream to keep paying their fair share. No more. No less.
Vote for Proposition 3.

Endorsement: Elect Michael Melillo to San Jose Unified School District Board of Education (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/30/endorsement-elect-michael-melillo-to-san-jose-unified-school-district-board-of-education/)
Endorsement: Reject San Mateo Community College District’s $848 million Measure V (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-reject-san-mateo-community-college-districts-848-million-measure-v/)
Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
In 2012, voters approved Proposition 30 to temporarily increase marginal rates on the top 2% of earners; and in 2016, they approved Proposition 55 to extend these same rates until 2030.
Now on the Nov. 3 ballot, Proposition 3 would keep these existing rates in place permanently after 2030.
The measure only applies to individuals whose incomes exceed $371,000 or joint filers whose incomes exceed $743,000. (The median full-time worker in California earns $65,000 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/who-are-californias-workers/). The median family’s income is $100,000 (https://data.census.gov/profile/California?g=040XX00US06).)
If Proposition 3 fails, the state’s General Fund would lose between $5 billion and $15 billion per year, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office projections (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Around 40% of those lost revenues would have gone to California’s public schools and colleges; the remainder would fund other state services, including healthcare, and the state’s rainy day reserve fund.
However, should it fail, the richest Californians would get a large windfall, the vast majority of which would flow to the top 1%.
Extremely disingenuous
The campaign against Proposition 3, sponsored by the California Taxpayers Association, ranges from merely misleading to downright scurrilous.
The main tactic used by the California Taxpayers Association, whose board of directors includes heads of the world’s biggest businesses, is to hide behind small businesses. Proposition 3, they argue, will hurt small business owners because “many” operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships and S Corps, and they report their business earnings on personal income taxes.
That might sound convincing until you look at Census and Franchise Tax Board data.
It turns out, the average revenue for the state’s nonemployer businesses — be they C corps, S corps, individual proprietorships, etc. — is less than $65,000. In other words, the vast majority of the state’s smallest businesses don’t make anywhere near enough to have to pay these higher rates. Invoking them, as opponents do, is absurd.
But what about prices. Will Proposition 3 raise prices and thus inflate inflation?
Opponents claim that small businesses will just pass the costs of this tax onto consumers. That might sound logical until you realize that Proposition 3 won’t raise taxes. It preserves existing ones.
Why would businesses suddenly raise prices because voters decided to maintain tax rates in place for the last 13 years?
They wouldn’t.
Perhaps the most dishonest attack on this progressive tax is that it will push the state’s wealthy out of the state and discourage investment.
Evidence from the last decade completely throws cold water on those fears of capital flight.
Millionaire factory
California’s share of the country’s millionaires and billionaires increased during the last decade (https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/CAwealthtax.pdf), as UC Berkeley’s Econometrics Lab found.
And Franchise Tax Board data show the same: The number of tax filers subject to the top tax rates more than doubled between 2013, when these higher rates went into effect, and 2024.
No serious economic analyst could look at the last decade and a half and call it an era of disinvestment or economic malaise in California. After all, this exact period saw California lead the planet in global investment, innovation and wealth creation. Our big companies — Apple, Alphabet, Meta, Netflix and Nvidia — became the biggest. And our early-stage startups, led by high-skilled talent, attracted historic levels of capital and then became globally dominant business behemoths, like Uber and Airbnb.
And that investment hasn’t stopped, just because the top 2% has been paying two or three percentage points more on their income taxes.
California’s startups attracted $366 billion from venture capitalists in the first six months of this year. (https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/californias-ai-dominance-fuels-366-billion-venture-capital-bonanza-820e9bde) Not only is that double its previous record but it’s three times the amount invested in the other 49 states combined. The total volume of capital invested in this one sector of the state in just half a year exceeds the annual economies of 25 states.
The fearmongering about these progressive taxes defies logic.
New urgency
Over the last year, the reason for keeping these rates in place has become even more urgent.
As a result of a vindictive Republican Congress and president, California will lose billions in federal funds. H.R. 1, or the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, is shifting the costs of maintaining our safety net back onto this state. California’s counties, which maintain the safety net, expect to lose as much as $9.5 billion per year (https://www.counties.org/hr1/https:/www.counties.org/hr1/).
Already, local governments, including Santa Clara County, are resorting to regressive sales taxes to prop up services once sustained with progressive federal taxes. Bay Area hospitals are seeing the number of uninsured in their emergency rooms double, as this news organization has documented.
Rejecting Proposition 3 would compound that problem, depriving the state of billions while handing a giant windfall to the Californians who need it least.
Proposition 40 was a different beast. (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/21/endorsement-reject-california-ballot-propositions-40-41-42-billionaires-tax-ai-inequality/) We opposed it. It was retroactive. It taxed wealth. It was new, and it does risk creating capital flight.
But Proposition 3 has none of those defects.
Vote yes.

California’s richest are doing great.
Over the last four decades, while the bottom four-fifths of households have seen their real incomes decline, the top 1% have seen their real incomes grow two and half times (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). This upper stratum now earns in a week what the middle fifth of Californians make in a year.
Proposition 3 asks the Californians truly living the California dream to keep paying their fair share. No more. No less.
Vote for Proposition 3.

In 2012, voters approved Proposition 30 to temporarily increase marginal rates on the top 2% of earners; and in 2016, they approved Proposition 55 to extend these same rates until 2030.
Now on the Nov. 3 ballot, Proposition 3 would keep these existing rates in place permanently after 2030.
The measure only applies to individuals whose incomes exceed $371,000 or joint filers whose incomes exceed $743,000. (The median full-time worker in California earns $65,000 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/who-are-californias-workers/). The median family’s income is $100,000 (https://data.census.gov/profile/California?g=040XX00US06).)
If Proposition 3 fails, the state’s General Fund would lose between $5 billion and $15 billion per year, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office projections (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Around 40% of those lost revenues would have gone to California’s public schools and colleges; the remainder would fund other state services, including healthcare, and the state’s rainy day reserve fund.
However, should it fail, the richest Californians would get a large windfall, the vast majority of which would flow to the top 1%.
Extremely disingenuous
The campaign against Proposition 3, sponsored by the California Taxpayers Association, ranges from merely misleading to downright scurrilous.
The main tactic used by the California Taxpayers Association, whose board of directors includes heads of the world’s biggest businesses, is to hide behind small businesses. Proposition 3, they argue, will hurt small business owners because “many” operate as sole proprietorships, partnerships and S Corps, and they report their business earnings on personal income taxes.
That might sound convincing until you look at Census and Franchise Tax Board data.
It turns out, the average revenue for the state’s nonemployer businesses — be they C corps, S corps, individual proprietorships, etc. — is less than $65,000. In other words, the vast majority of the state’s smallest businesses don’t make anywhere near enough to have to pay these higher rates. Invoking them, as opponents do, is absurd.
But what about prices. Will Proposition 3 raise prices and thus inflate inflation?
Opponents claim that small businesses will just pass the costs of this tax onto consumers. That might sound logical until you realize that Proposition 3 won’t raise taxes. It preserves existing ones.
Why would businesses suddenly raise prices because voters decided to maintain tax rates in place for the last 13 years?
They wouldn’t.
Perhaps the most dishonest attack on this progressive tax is that it will push the state’s wealthy out of the state and discourage investment.
Evidence from the last decade completely throws cold water on those fears of capital flight.
Millionaire factory
California’s share of the country’s millionaires and billionaires increased during the last decade (https://eml.berkeley.edu/~saez/CAwealthtax.pdf), as UC Berkeley’s Econometrics Lab found.
And Franchise Tax Board data show the same: The number of tax filers subject to the top tax rates more than doubled between 2013, when these higher rates went into effect, and 2024.
No serious economic analyst could look at the last decade and a half and call it an era of disinvestment or economic malaise in California. After all, this exact period saw California lead the planet in global investment, innovation and wealth creation. Our big companies — Apple, Alphabet, Meta, Netflix and Nvidia — became the biggest. And our early-stage startups, led by high-skilled talent, attracted historic levels of capital and then became globally dominant business behemoths, like Uber and Airbnb.
And that investment hasn’t stopped, just because the top 2% has been paying two or three percentage points more on their income taxes.
California’s startups attracted $366 billion from venture capitalists in the first six months of this year. (https://www.wsj.com/tech/ai/californias-ai-dominance-fuels-366-billion-venture-capital-bonanza-820e9bde) Not only is that double its previous record but it’s three times the amount invested in the other 49 states combined. The total volume of capital invested in this one sector of the state in just half a year exceeds the annual economies of 25 states.
The fearmongering about these progressive taxes defies logic.
New urgency
Over the last year, the reason for keeping these rates in place has become even more urgent.
As a result of a vindictive Republican Congress and president, California will lose billions in federal funds. H.R. 1, or the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, is shifting the costs of maintaining our safety net back onto this state. California’s counties, which maintain the safety net, expect to lose as much as $9.5 billion per year (https://www.counties.org/hr1/https:/www.counties.org/hr1/).
Already, local governments, including Santa Clara County, are resorting to regressive sales taxes to prop up services once sustained with progressive federal taxes. Bay Area hospitals are seeing the number of uninsured in their emergency rooms double, as this news organization has documented.
Rejecting Proposition 3 would compound that problem, depriving the state of billions while handing a giant windfall to the Californians who need it least.
Proposition 40 was a different beast. (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/21/endorsement-reject-california-ballot-propositions-40-41-42-billionaires-tax-ai-inequality/) We opposed it. It was retroactive. It taxed wealth. It was new, and it does risk creating capital flight.
But Proposition 3 has none of those defects.
Vote yes.

I've got the main findings on the debate now. The Rauh and Shyu study, a peer-reviewed paper, found that Prop 30 led a small share of top-bracket earners to leave the state, and that those who stayed reduced their income, with responses eroding a large part of the windfall within two years.

Now I'm weighing the two studies against each other: Varner, Young, and Prohofsky found only a very slight difference in high-earner migration, while Rauh says they undercount movers because of how they define it. I'm also checking the windfall figures, since the earlier 55.6% number came from a previous version and the published paper gives 45.2% and 60.9% within two years. The critics' counter-evidence on rising top-rate filers and millionaire shares is an argument from the Yes side, so I don't think it counts as a rigorous rebuttal.

I'm checking whether the LAO's $5–15 billion estimate for Prop 3 treats the revenue as static, since Hoover calls it effectively static. I'd like to find out what assumptions the LAO's fiscal analysis actually makes, so I'm looking at its earlier analyses of Prop 55 and Prop 30.

I'm checking whether the LAO's Prop 3 estimate accounts for taxpayer behavior, since its pre-ballot fiscal analysis for AG #25-0016 might say so. The erosion figures suggest the net revenue could land well below the static $5–15 billion, depending on whether the remaining rates behave like the 2012 increase did.

So if the Rauh and Shyu erosion applies, Prop 3's net revenue could fall well below the static $5–15 billion. If about half the windfall erodes over the long run, the net gain would be roughly $2.5–7.5 billion a year.

I'm weighing whether Rauh's claim holds up: he says net revenue from the top rates has been negative since 2018, which would mean departures and base erosion cost more than the remaining high earners pay. I'd need evidence for that, and the Mercury News figure on filer counts doesn't settle it, since it tracks the number of filers rather than revenue. I'm also noting that the erosion may be partly timing, so the two-year figure may not reflect the long-run effect.

I'm checking whether the LAO's $5–15 billion estimate accounts for behavioral responses, since that decides how much revenue is really at stake. If it assumes none, the Rauh and Shyu erosion suggests the real figure could be much lower. I'll look at the LAO's Prop 55 analysis and its pre-ballot review of AG #25-0016, and also at the surcharge revenue actually collected in recent budgets.

I'm now checking the $104 billion figure from the initiative's findings against the LAO's annual estimates, since roughly $7.5 billion a year over fourteen years would land close to it. Then I'm turning to the Yes side's claim that top-rate filers doubled between 2013 and 2024, which I want to test for whether it reflects real income growth or something else.

Now I'm turning to the Prop 98 fungibility question and the Yes side's claim that the money is locked in for schools. The LAO puts the figure at 40%, and the initiative's language says the funds are continuously appropriated and cannot be suspended or withheld, so the allocation is fixed in the constitution. That also means voters can't revisit it later without another amendment, which protects schools from budget cuts but removes flexibility if priorities change.

I'm now checking whether Prop 3's conflict clause reaches Prop 40, the billionaire tax, since CalMatters groups the other two tax measures apart from the wealth tax. Props 41 and 42 look like business-backed counters, so I need to confirm what each of them actually does to personal income tax rates.

I'm checking whether Prop 40, the billionaire tax, actually conflicts with Prop 3, since it's a one-time wealth levy rather than a personal income rate. The CalMatters explainer should show whether it's described as touching income tax, so I'll pull that up.

I'm now going through the Yes side's ballot claims about Prop 3, starting with the assertion that it is not a new tax and raises taxes on no one. That holds for today's rates, but the measure would make the current rates permanent when they would otherwise expire, so the framing looks misleading for later years. The claim that Prop 3 stops millionaires and billionaires from getting a tax cut is accurate against the expiring rates. I'm about to check the third claim, which warns of billions in cuts and teacher layoffs for millions of students if the measure fails.

I'm checking the Prop 98 side of this: the LAO's 40% figure means schools would lose about 40% of any revenue shortfall, roughly $2–6 billion, and the guarantee is formula-based, so the state could backfill but isn't required to. That makes the "billions in cuts" claim roughly right without being automatic. I'm also looking at the audit and money-reaches-classrooms claims, since the text supports the audits but the fungibility rule means the state could cut its own school spending by the same amount.

I'm checking how the Yes side's claims hold up against the LAO's 40% figure. The Prop 98 fungibility means the EPA money does reach schools, but the net gain is smaller than the "billions" framing suggests. I'm also weighing the Hoover claim about Prop 30 funding pensions, which is a separate and contested point.

I'm checking how the No side's claim of a "largest permanent income tax increase" compares against the LAO's upper estimate of about $15 billion a year, since that figure is the cost in a strong market year rather than a typical one. The Medi-Cal point also needs care: the only earmark is the capped health allocation of up to $2 billion, so the claim that the freed-up money helps Medi-Cal is directionally fair but not guaranteed.

I'm checking the No side's three claims: the "largest permanent tax increase" line and the $30 billion deficit figure are rhetorical and I can't verify them, and the nation's-highest-taxes claim holds for income tax but I still need to confirm the gas tax comparison.

I'm weighing whether California's sales tax is actually the highest in the nation, since the state rate is only 7.25% even if local combined rates run high. The gas excise tax claim seems right, but I'd want to check the sales tax comparison before counting it as a factual error. I'm now weighing the consequences of a no vote: a gross hole of roughly $5–15B a year from 2031, plus about $2–6B a year in school funding unless the Legislature backfills it. I'm also considering the case for keeping the top rates as a way to avoid those cuts, which turns on whether the top rates should stay high.

I'm weighing the case for Prop 3 more directly now: the strongest points are that it avoids a scheduled loss of roughly $5–15B a year in a budget already projecting deficits, protects about $2–6B a year for K-14 schools, and touches only the top 2% of earners. The main downside I keep returning to is that a constitutional rate would be hard to revisit, which makes the state's budget more reliant on a volatile revenue source.

I'm now weighing the case against Prop 3: it would lock a temporary-sounding tax into the constitution where only voters can change it, and the revenue depends heavily on capital gains from the top 2%. The behavioral research points to substantial erosion, and only about 40% of the money reaches schools, so the direct school benefit may be smaller than the Yes side suggests.

I'm weighing the strongest case for "No": the research suggests large behavioral erosion, and only about 40% of the revenue reaches schools. Even so, Rauh-Shyu still show the top rates netting positive, so the real question is whether that net is worth the efficiency and fairness costs. That turns on values, not just the numbers.

I'm weighing whether an impartial analyst would lean toward "No," given the constitutional lock-in and the absence of a sunset, and recalling how some editorial boards opposed the earlier extension on volatility grounds.

I'm weighing how the Chronicle's endorsement fits with the other papers: it backs Prop 3 on the view that California can't afford to cut ongoing school and health funding, even if that money is unstable. Fiscal conservatives and business groups are the ones leaning no, and their concerns about temporary taxes, lock-in, and spending growth are legitimate. The real choice seems to come down to whether keeping this revenue outweighs the lock-in concern, and that depends on how someone weighs those values.

I'm weighing whether a "Yes" or "No" would be the better call, and which mistake would cost more. If I say Yes and the net revenue is around $3–8B, the schools and health care funding that's at stake gets protected, though the top rates stay permanently high and some high earners may leave or cut their income. Saying No would rest on the lock-in and the overstated revenue, but the budget counterfactual makes that harder to justify.

I'm weighing the case against a "No" vote: if the measure fails, the state loses roughly $5–15B a year starting in 2031, and schools lose $2–6B of that, which would widen deficits and force painful cuts. A lower top rate might keep some high earners, but the evidence suggests the state wouldn't gain much from that. The budget consequences of expiration look like the larger concern.

I'm noting that the state's budget is already running structural deficits, and the No side's answer is to cut spending first, though most of the big spending is locked in by formula. I'm leaning toward Yes, while keeping in mind that a permanent rate weakens future flexibility.

I'm weighing the cost of a No vote against the Yes costs: if Prop 3 fails, schools would lose roughly $2–6B and the rest of the budget another $3–9B, likely hitting Medi-Cal and higher education. Set against a permanent tax on the top 2% of earners, that makes the balance tilt toward Yes for many voters, though the net revenue estimates remain contested.

I'm checking whether the measure's constitutional language creates any side effects, such as how the Legislature could interact with it. I also want to see whether the proponent-standing clause or the conflicting-measure clause could change the outcome if another tax measure on the ballot passes with more votes.

I'm checking whether Prop 3's conflicting-measure clause could knock out a competing tax measure, like Prop 40, if both pass and Prop 3 gets more votes. To judge that, I need the Props 40–43 descriptions from the CalMatters "5 tax measures" article to see which ones actually touch personal income tax rates.

I'm going to check whether Prop 3's conflicting-measure clause could void a competing tax measure, since that would affect how the Props 40–42 interplay matters. I'll pull the CalMatters descriptions to confirm, and I'll also confirm that the constitutional lock means only voters can change the rates.

I'm checking the Prop 3 summary against the rest of the research: it's a constitutional amendment, so only voters can change it, and I've already gathered the official guide, the LAO analysis, and several editorial and polling sources.

I'm now checking the CalMatters rundown of Props 40–43 to see whether any of them touch personal income tax rates, since Prop 3's conflicting-measure clause would matter there. I also want to test the EdSource claim that small businesses would be hit, comparing it against the $371k and $743k thresholds and the pass-through figures.

I'm now weighing whether the small-business effects are as broad as EdSource suggests. The top rates only reach owners above the $371k and $743k thresholds, so the impact is real but limited to high-income owners rather than millions of businesses.

I'm noting that the PPIC partisan split shows Democrats largely backing Prop 3 and Republicans largely opposing it. I'm also thinking through the CTA angle: CalMatters reports that a failed vote wouldn't end the push, since the union would have two more chances, likely in 2028 and 2030.

I'm checking the LAO's overview of the spending plan, which projects operating deficits narrowing to about $8–10B a year after 2026-27 but staying notable throughout the forecast period.

I'm checking the LAO's budget outlook, where the operating deficits look like roughly $8–10B a year through 2029-30 under the administration's estimates. Those projections stop before the rates expire, so the 2031 revenue drop would fall outside the forecast window and widen the gap further.

I'm checking the LAO's projections, which put operating deficits at about $8–10 billion a year through 2029–30, a window that closes before a 2031 expiration would take effect. If the rates lapsed then, the state could lose roughly $5–15 billion a year on top of those deficits, a strong point for Yes, though the net figure could be smaller once behavioral responses are counted.

I'm checking the roughly $10B-a-year figure for the higher rates, which the CalMatters piece and the Mercury News op-ed both cite. I'm also confirming the LAO's point that the top combined rate is the highest in the nation, and that the top-earning taxpayers pay about half of state income taxes. Next I'm looking at the Varner, Young, and Prohofsky paper on migration, which Hoover characterizes as finding only a very slight effect from the 2012 increase, and whether Rauh's critique of it holds up.

I'm going to check the CalMatters tax measures article to confirm the descriptions of Props 40–43 and the CTA's point that a failed vote would leave two more chances. I also want to find a neutral source for the Varner, Young, and Prohofsky migration study, since Stanford's own framing says Prop 30 did raise revenue, just less than the static estimates.

content.text: The Legislative Analyst's Prop 55 numbers and the Budget Center's realized-revenue figures help calibrate the estimates. I'll check two remaining items: CalMatters' overview of the other tax measures, to see whether any of them interacts with Prop 3's conflicting-measures clause, and the Legislative Analyst's August 2026 budget overview for the deficit trajectory.

5 tax measures are on the California ballot. Here’s how to make sense of them all
by
Ben Christopher (https://calmatters.org/author/ben-christopher/)
October 5, 2026 October 4, 2026

In summary
California voters haven’t had to make so many decisions about tax policy at the ballot since 1990. Our analysis shows voters tend to reject new taxes.
Welcome to CalMatters, the only nonprofit newsroom devoted solely to covering issues that affect all Californians. Sign up for WhatMatters (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/whatmatters) to receive the latest news and commentary on the most important issues in the Golden State.
California voters will soon be asked whether they want to keep taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) the incomes of the rich.
And they’ll be asked whether to start taxing (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) the accumulated wealth of the even richer.
Wait, there’s more. They’ll also get to weigh in on whether we should ban wealth taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) altogether, subject the money raised by future taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) to a state spending cap and make it harder for voters to pass certain local taxes (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/).
That doesn’t include any of the other propositions on the November ballot that are likely to affect the state budget. Nor does it include the roughly 300 (https://www.caltax.org/elections/local-tax-elections/2026-Local-Elections.pdf?_gl=1*pjll0w*_ga*NTYyOTYwNzgyLjE3NzYyODUwNTE.*_ga_RR9B893WL0*czE3OTA3MjI1MTEkbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGo0MyRsMCRoMA..*_ga_98RV0P0X7N*czE3OTA3MjI1MDckbzgxJGcxJHQxNzkwNzIyNTI4JGozOSRsMCRoMA..) tax and bond measures that will be popping up in local elections across the state.
And you thought tax season only came in April.
With 14 measures in total, the 2026 California ballot (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) is a busy one. Voters haven’t been presented with this many choices in a decade. It’s an especially active year for tax-related measures — those that hike taxes, cut them, introduce new ones, jettison old ones or change the rules by which taxes are approved and enacted.
Five of those are on the ballot this time around, the most since 1990.
Altogether they have the potential to reshape the state’s finances, beef up or starve some of our largest public spending programs, change the rules around taxation and — if opponents of the proposed wealth tax (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) are to be believed — trigger a Randian exodus of the state’s wellest-to-do.
The ‘black hole’ on the ballot
Though five tax measures are on the ballot, voters are really just seeing three big questions.
The first: Should California be the first state in the nation to introduce a wealth tax?
That question is “the black hole into which all political energy is going right now,” said Jon Coupal, president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, a group that advocates for low taxes.

Three measures — Propositions 40, 41 and 42 — provide opposing answers.
Prop. 40 would slap every Californian with a net worth of at least $1 billion (all approximately 200 of them) with a one-time 5% tax on their wealth, excluding real estate and retirement accounts.
This isn’t an income tax, which skims off a share of a person’s earnings, but a tax on the assessed, unrealized value of investments. Think of this like the property tax that homeowners pay on their houses, except it applies to stocks, bonds, business shares, Bugattis and the occasional machine gun collection (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/#:~:text=machine%20gun%20collection).
A sign displayed at the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco on Feb. 21, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo
The Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the measure has the potential to raise tens of billions of dollars. Almost all of it would be set aside for the state’s public health insurance programs, which are bracing for dramatic federal cuts (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/08/medi-cal-the-cut-healthcare-threatened/).
That’s assuming the measure passes and survives the blizzard of inevitable legal challenges (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/31/opinion-why-flawed-wealth-tax-could-backfire-on-california/). Though a number of countries (https://taxfoundation.org/data/all/eu/wealth-taxes-europe/) have introduced wealth taxes at either the national or regional level, California’s would be the first in the United States.
No surprise, many of the state’s billionaires are pushing back hard. They’re doing that in the usual way, with literally hundreds of millions of dollars in campaign spending. But they’re also doing it with two additional measures on the ballot itself. Prop. 41 would, among other things (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/), ban the state from collecting taxes that circumvent a 1970s state spending limit (https://calmatters.org/politics/2021/05/newsom-tax-rebate/), which Prop. 40 is written to do.
Prop. 42 would ban new taxes on financial assets, private businesses and most other forms of wealth outright — an explicit reversal of Prop. 40.
If both the wealth tax and either of the countermeasures are approved by the voters, the one with the higher vote tally becomes law. That’s why the wealth tax could go down in defeat even if a majority of voters support it (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/).
But voters shouldn’t think of Props. 41 and 42 as mere “no” votes on Prop. 40, said Kayla Kitson, a tax policy analyst at the California Budget & Policy Center, a left-leaning think tank. Prop. 41 would also require the state’s auditor to conduct a “pre-election” analysis of any program set to be funded by a future tax measure and then make recommendations on how to cut costs by 10%.
Beyond banning future wealth taxes, Prop. 42 would also prevent future taxes from applying retroactively before a tax is approved. That could remove the state’s ability to keep people or businesses from avoiding a tax they know is coming, said Kitson.
Two more tax questions
The other two tax measures have nothing to do with the wealth tax. One would make permanent a boosted income tax rate for higher earners. The other would make it harder for local governments to raise certain taxes in the future.
The high-earner tax is the third, and possibly final, installment in a decade-long electoral trilogy.
First proposed by former Gov. Jerry Brown as a temporary (https://repository.uclawsf.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2308&context=ca_ballot_props) solution to fund education in the fiscal hangover of the Great Recession, the measure sticks a higher tax bracket on the state’s top 2% of earners (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)). Re-authorized by voters in 2016, the tax has (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_55,_Extension_of_the_Proposition_30_Income_Tax_Increase_(2016)) generated between $5 billion and $16 billion annually (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). Most of that money has gone to schools.
The tax expires in 2030, which is why the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest K-12 public school educators’ union, was eager to put its permanent renewal on the ballot this year. If it fails, the union will have two more chances.
Hence, Proposition 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/), which would make the boosted tax rates for individually earned income above $360,000 per year a perpetual part of the state’s tax code.
Proposition 43 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-43-tax-threshold/)’s backstory also goes back nearly a decade.
The measure would hike the share of votes needed to pass certain local taxes. Specifically, these are taxes that raise money for a specific program (https://debtguide-api.treasurer.ca.gov/guide-pages/chapter-1-legally-incurring-debt-state-law-restrictions-on-public-agency-debt-and-revenues/1-4-local-government-revenue-sources-security-for-and-repayment-of-debt/1-4-6-special-taxes) or purpose and that are placed on the ballot by citizen signature-gathering efforts, as opposed to local elected officials. If Prop. 43 passes, this very particular type of tax would need the support of at least two-thirds of local voters.
Business groups and anti-tax advocates have been wanting to put some version of Prop. 43 on the ballot since 2017 (https://calmatters.org/economy/2017/08/california-taxes-two-step/) when the state Supreme Court ruled that so-called citizen-initiated special taxes only need a simple majority of the vote to pass. The anti-tax advocates got close two years ago, but were stymied by another court ruling (https://calmatters.org/politics/2024/06/california-taxes-supreme-court-ballot/). This year, the measure finally made it, but only after negotiations with the Democrats (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/06/tax-cut-measure-pulled/) in the Legislature pared it down, applying the rule to future taxes only.
California tax measures tend to fail
This all makes for a tremendously confusing voting experience for most Californians.
That’s probably bad news for the supporters of these measures, since uncertain voters tend to err on the side of “no,” said Mark Baldassare, survey director at the Public Policy Institute of California.
“When voters aren’t sure how to proceed, staying with the status quo and letting someone else decide at a later date is a safe bet,” he said.
That may partly explain why tax measures, which are inherently complicated and tend to come with unpredictable consequences, fare especially poorly on the ballot. Since 2000, a solid majority (57%) of non-tax ballot measures have passed compared to a mere third of tax propositions.
The sheer number of open questions (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/california-billionaire-tax-explainer/) surrounding the proposed wealth tax (Is it constitutional? Can the state effectively implement it? Will all the billionaires flee to Florida?) puts it on shakier footing with an electorate that tends to reject uncertainty, said Baldassare. A narrow majority of 52% percent of likely voters said they supported the measure in a recent PPIC poll.
The tax on high earners in Prop. 3, may face better odds because it makes permanent an existing tax rather than introducing a new one. In the same poll, 58% of likely voters indicated that they would support the measure.
“When people see the words ‘renew’ or ‘extend’ it gives them a sense that this is the status quo, we’re not being asked to make a change here,” he said.
But Prop. 3’s backers shouldn’t take too much comfort in that. Support for propositions tend to decline (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2019/10/ballot-california-polling-trend-slump-fact-check-myth-data/) as Election Day approaches. The sheer number of tax measures on offer could also inflict voters with “tax fatigue” leading them to vote “no” across the board, said Baldassare.
Then there’s the general political vibe.
Earlier this year, PPIC asked a sample of Californians whether they preferred lower taxes and fewer services or higher taxes and more services.
Fifty-five percent said they’d prefer the lower tax bill (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/).
For the record: An earlier version of this article misstated the last time voters were presented with five or more tax-related measures on the same California ballot. The most recent year was 1990, not 1994.

INTRODUCTION
Each year, our office publishes the California
Spending Plan to summarize the annual state
budget. In this publication we provide an overview
of the 2026-27 budget package, give a brief
description of how the budget process unfolded,
and then highlight the major features of the
budget approved by the Legislature and signed
by the Governor. This publication reflects the
administration’s estimates of legislative actions
taken through the end of June 2026. In addition to
this report, we will release a series of issue-specific,
online posts that give more detail on the major
actions in the budget package.
BUDGET CHOICES
In most years, we would describe the size of the
budget problem (or budget surplus) the Legislature
addressed (or allocated) and the mix of choices
that make up that total. This year, neither framing
fits the budget package as neatly. Although the
budget package includes some traditional budget
solutions, it also reflects a substantial amount of
new discretionary spending and a large, first-time
deposit into a surplus holding account. Taken
together, these choices roughly offset one another.
At the same time, the budget continues to rely on
reserve capacity, even as revenues have surged to
levels only surpassed by the state’s previous peak
in 2021-22. Taken altogether, this makes the budget
condition difficult to describe concisely. As such,
this section describes the state’s budget choices
on both sides of the ledger: first new commitments
and discretionary choices, and then the budget
solutions made.
NEW COMMITMENTS
Revenue and Spending Commitments
New Discretionary Spending Totals Nearly
$6 Billion. The budget commits $5.7 billion
in new, discretionary General Fund money in
2026-27. We define discretionary spending as
new spending or revenue reductions that were
not previously authorized under current law or
legislative policy. Nearly all of these commitments
are spending related—revenue reductions account
for only about $25 million of the total, mainly a
temporary reduction in the minimum franchise
tax for newly formed businesses. For context,
this new discretionary spending is equivalent to
roughly 90 percent of the total year-over-year
growth in General Fund spending between 2025-26
and 2026-27. A list of the discretionary General

(1988)) in the 2026-27 budget package are listed

Most New Spending Is One Time, but the
Budget Also Added New Ongoing Costs.
Of the $5.7 billion in new discretionary spending,
about $5 billion (87 percent) is one time, while the
remaining roughly $700 million reflects ongoing
commitments—costs that will recur as part of
the budget’s baseline in future years. On a fully
phased-in basis, these will total about $825 million
annually. This new ongoing spending is a relatively
small share of the total. Nonetheless, it adds to the
budget’s baseline costs in future years, offsetting
the solutions described elsewhere in this report that
were used to address the gap between the state’s
ongoing revenues and expenditures.
New Spending Is Concentrated in Health,
Though New Spending Touches Nearly Every
Program Area. With over 250 individual items,
new discretionary spending reaches nearly
every part of the budget, but on a programmatic
basis, health programs account for the largest
share (nearly 40 percent of the total), followed
by general government, labor, and related
programs (15 percent); housing and homelessness
(12 percent); and criminal justice (11 percent).
Human services and resources and environment
programs each account for about 8 percent
to 9 percent, with the remainder split between
higher education (3 percent), K-14 education
(excluding Proposition 98) (2 percent), and
