PROP. 3 KEEPS THE TAX RATES THE TOP 2% HAVE PAID FOR THE PAST 15 YEARS AND DOES NOT RAISE YOUR TAXES.
Prop. 3 maintains the current tax rates the wealthiest 2% of Californians have been paying for 15 years, ensuring couples that earn more than $740,000 continue to pay their fair share.
WITHOUT PROP. 3 MILLIONAIRES AND BILLIONAIRES GET A MASSIVE TAX CUT—AND THE REST OF US PAY FOR IT.
Teacher and staff layoffs, overcrowded classrooms and fewer counselors in our schools; cuts to Medi-Cal, children’s healthcare and the clinics families rely on; and less for the firefighters, emergency response and wildfire protection that keep our communities safe.
PROP. 3 HAS STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND FUNDS EDUCATION DIRECTLY.
Prop. 3’s funding goes straight to local schools and community colleges. Sacramento politicians cannot touch it or redirect it. Not one penny may be spent on bureaucracy or administrative overhead. Every dollar is independently audited every year, districts must post their spending online, and any official who misuses the money faces prosecution and criminal penalties.
PROP. 3 PROTECTS HEALTHCARE AND FIRE PROTECTION.
By guaranteeing funding for our classrooms, Prop. 3 ensures California can also invest in Medi-Cal and children’s healthcare, and in the firefighters and wildfire protection our communities depend on. That’s why teachers, school employees, nurses and firefighters agree: VOTE YES ON PROPOSITION 3.

Next I'm checking which measures are on the 2026 ballot, since the No side's warnings about health insurance and software taxes may belong to a separate billionaire-tax initiative rather than Prop 3 itself.

I'm going to pull up the full text of the measure's PDF next, since it's long and I need the details on how the school allocation actually works.

(a) In 2012, California voters passed a tax increase on
high-income earners—the top 2%—to fund critical
state services and stave off extreme cuts to public
education brought on by the fiscal challenges of the
Great Recession. These tax rates were extended by the
voters in 2016, with 63% voting yes. Since its initial
passage, this tax measure has raised more than $104
billion for schools and other essential services. It is a
foundational part of the state budget and the state
Rainy Day Fund.

to make important investments in the education and

public school system become more competitive among
the 50 states. In 2012, California ranked in the bottom
10 among the states in school spending. Today, with
these revenues, California has made real progress in
school spending. Our state now provides free school
meals; free transitional kindergarten to all four-year-
olds; free before-and-after school care for younger
elementary students; and community services in many
school districts.
(c) Unless the tax is extended by the voters, it will
expire in 2030. That would result in an immediate
reduction to state revenues of over $10 billion and
devastating cuts to schools, children’s health care, and
other essential services. It would reverse the gains our
schools have made since the initial passage of the high-
earner income tax in 2012.
(d) This measure does not increase taxes on couples
earning less than $680,000 or individuals earning less
than $340,000, in today’s dollars. It does not change
the existing tax rates, which have remained the same
since this tax measure was first enacted in 2012.
(e) This is not the time to be giving the wealthiest
people in California a tax cut that they don’t need and
that our schools and communities can’t afford.
Maintaining this tax on high earners helps ensure that
California children receive the education and health
care they need to thrive and achieve their highest
potential, while allowing this tax to expire would require
major cuts to the education and health of our next
generation.
(f) California’s future depends on the success of its
over 9 million children. Every California child deserves
a fair chance to become a successful adult. But for
children to succeed as adults, they must have access
to high quality education and health care.
(g) For children, education and health care are
essential and dependent on one another. Access to a
quality education is fundamental to the success of
California’s children. Even with adequate schools,
children cannot obtain an education if illness prevents
them from attending. And children growing up in
communities without adequate health care are more
likely to contract illnesses or have chronic medical
conditions that prevent them from regularly attending
school.
(h) Research shows that early access to quality
education and health care improves children’s chances

the education and health care they need to thrive and

Day Fund to prevent cuts to health care for children

budget swings over the past 15 years, with good years

low-income Californians, and especially on our
children. But federal tax laws are giving huge tax breaks

I'm checking how Section 4 ties into Section 36 of Article XIII, since the Prop 3 text carries over the Prop 30 Education Protection Account language with the dates shifted to 2031. I also want to note that the Education Protection Account gets the tax revenue, split 89% to K-12 and 11% to community colleges.

I'm working out how the 50% remainder allocation to child health care, capped at $2 billion a year, sits alongside the EPA's school funding. I'm also weighing whether the earlier Prop 30 structure already routed excess revenue that way.

I'm recalling that under Prop 30 the EPA revenue is used for schools, and that it counts toward the Prop 98 minimum guarantee. That means the money isn't entirely new for schools, and the state could free up General Fund money for other uses, like Medi-Cal for children.

I'm noting that the EPA revenue counts toward the Prop 98 guarantee, so the state's General Fund obligation to schools drops, leaving money for other uses like children's health care. The LAO's figure of roughly 40 percent going to schools fits that, and I want to check their full Prop 3 analysis to confirm the net effect.

I'm noticing that Section 5 sets up a conflicting-measures rule: if another measure affecting personal income tax rates lands on the same ballot with more yes votes, Prop 3 prevails and the other is void. I want to check whether a competing measure like that is actually on the 2026 ballot, and I also see Section 7 gives proponents standing to defend the measure if the state won't.

I'm going to pull the rest of the Prop 3 text, since the document cut off before the final section. I'm also looking for which parts are new versus carried over from the existing constitutional language, because the formatting that would show that is missing.

I'm recalling that Prop 55 probably set up the children's health care allocation, which would mean Prop 3 mostly carries that forward. I'm also thinking about what happens if Prop 3 fails: the high-income rates would expire after 2030, so the question is how much revenue that actually removes.

I'm weighing the case for Prop 3 here: it would keep roughly $5 to 15 billion a year flowing to schools and health care, avoid a big tax cut for the top earners, and the high-income rates have already been in place for about fifteen years.

I'm weighing the case against Prop 3 now: it would make a temporary tax permanent, leave the state reliant on the top 2% of earners who already pay about half of income taxes, and possibly push some high earners out. I'm also questioning whether the new school money is as large as advertised, since some of it may simply replace General Fund spending.

Next I'm looking for the broader context on Prop 3: the LAO's full analysis, how the new money compares to freed-up General Fund spending, the state's budget outlook, and polling and editorial positions. I'll also check whether a competing tax measure is on the ballot that could trigger the conflicting-measures clause in Section 5.

Proposition 3
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
Analysis of Measure
Background
Most State Money Comes From the Income Tax. The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for most spending from the state's main operating account, the General Fund. The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend Its Money? This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public. About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, courts, and other state services.
Proposal
Proposition 3 makes the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
Fiscal Effects
Proposition 3 Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by Proposition 3 will go up and down a lot from year to year. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing income that is closely tied to the stock market, which is always changing. In a weak year, the proposition might bring in around $5 billion in revenue to the state. In a strong year, the proposition might bring in $15 billion in revenue to the state. In most years, revenue would be in between these amounts.
Funding for Education and Other Programs. Proposition 3 results in funding for education and other programs. Roughly 40 percent of the funding would go to schools and community colleges. The rest would go to other state programs. Part of this amount would be set aside in budget reserves the state could use to fund these programs when revenues decline.
Yes/No Statement
A YES vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would become permanent instead of expiring in 2031.
A NO vote on this measure means: An income tax increase on high-income earners in place since 2012 would expire in 2031.
Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact
Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income tax revenue by making a temporary tax increase on high-income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031.

PROP 3: The Permanent High-Income Tax Initiative
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%203.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Analysis & Assessment
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Summary
Proposition 3 would take the Prop 30 higher personal income tax rates on top earners and make them permanent. Voters approved Prop 30 as a temporary measure in 2012 to close a budget shortfall. The measure was then extended in 2016 under Prop 55. Under current law the increased taxes expire after the 2030 tax year, so a yes vote is, in effect, a tax increase from 2031 onward compared with the law as it now stands. Hoover Institution research on the 2012 rate increase found that high earners’ responses to the higher tax rates, either by leaving the state or reporting less income, erased much of the revenue the higher rates were expected to raise.
Other Hoover Institution research shows that California’s budget already depends to an unusual degree on a small, mobile group of taxpayers whose income tends to be dependent on stock market performance. It also finds that much of the money raised for schools has been absorbed by rising pension costs rather than reaching classrooms.
Proposition 3 would enshrine into the state constitution increased fiscal dependence on a variable tax with no future date for voters to revisit the decision.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0016).
Type: Initiative constitutional amendment
A vote YES means: The temporary higher personal income tax rates on top earners become permanent instead of expiring after the 2030 tax year. Taxable income above about $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers (2025 tax brackets, adjusted annually for inflation) would continue to face marginal rates of 10.3 to 12.3 percent and of 13.3 percent on income above $1 million.
A vote NO means: The higher tax rates expire on schedule. Beginning in 2031, the top rate would return to 9.3 percent (plus the separate 1 percent income tax surcharge on income above $1 million, for a combined top rate of 10.3 percent).
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0016, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf)
LAO analysis: Proposition 3, Legislative Analyst’s Office (PDF) (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf)
1. Overview
Proposition 3 would remove the expiration date on the higher personal income tax rates that California voters first approved as Proposition 30 in 2012. These temporary taxes were intended to forestall additional education budget cuts in the wake of tax revenue declines following the Great Recession. They were set to expire after 2018, but Proposition 55 in 2016 extended the taxes through 2030 and added the formula for the taxes to fund Medi-Cal when revenues exceed specific benchmarks.
Now Prop 3 would make these taxes—1, 2, and 3 percentage point surcharges on top of the state’s 9.3 percent bracket—permanent. Combined with the separate 1 percent surcharge tax on personal income above $1 million (created by Proposition 63 in 2004), the Prop 30 income tax surcharges give California the highest top marginal personal income tax rate in the nation, at 13.3 percent. This rises further to 14.6 percent on wage income once the now-uncapped state disability insurance payroll tax is included.
These income tax surcharges fall on roughly the top 2 percent of tax filers in any given year, a group that already pays about half of all state income taxes. Because much of their income comes from highly variable capital gains, stock options, and business sales, the Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) expects the revenue at stake to swing between about $5 billion in a weak year and $15 billion in a strong year.
Supporters stress that Proposition 3 does not raise anyone’s rate this year. That is true—but incomplete. Current law already schedules these rates to end after 2030, so the relevant comparison is not today’s tax bill but the one taxpayers would face in 2031. Measured against current law, a yes vote raises taxes on affected earners from that point forward, permanently. The LAO’s own description of a yes vote is that “an income tax increase on high-income earners” would become permanent.
Despite Prop 30 originally being advertised as necessary to avoid education funding cuts, the tax doesn’t provide as much additional state funding for schools as would be expected on the surface. The tax revenue flows into the state’s general fund and is held in the Education Protection Account (EPA), whereupon it is disbursed to schools (89 percent) and community colleges (11 percent). However, because the EPA counts as general fund revenue, and Prop 98 only mandates (under the formula currently in effect) that about 40 percent of the general fund goes to education, only about 40 percent of Prop 30’s tax revenue actually represents an increase to school funding. Except for special circumstances, the remaining 60 percent of the EPA doesn’t necessarily increase school-related expenditures because those dollars count toward the Prop 98 guarantee. This means that policymakers can use the funding to replace other obligatory general fund education expenditures on a dollar-for-dollar basis.
In years when the state’s general fund revenues exceed both the Proposition 98 education spending guarantee and the cost of maintaining existing state programs, half of the excess (up to $2 billion, as stipulated by Prop 55) goes to Medi-Cal health services. The remainder supports other general fund programs and budget reserves. In summary, what was initially framed as a temporary tax to avoid cuts to education funding has shifted to effectively become ordinary California tax revenue and is poised to become permanent.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0016, “The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0016%20%28%26quot%3BThe%20California%20Children%26%23039%3Bs%20Education%20and%20Health%20Care%20Protection%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (filed August 29, 2025).
Key language:
The important change is actually the deletion of the expiration date for the higher tax brackets.
What it amends: Section 36 of Article XIII of the California Constitution, the section created by Proposition 30 and extended by Proposition 55. Because the change is constitutional, the legislature cannot repeal or reduce the rates—only another statewide vote could change the tax rates.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
A permanent extension of the 1, 2, and 3 percentage point personal income tax surcharges on high earners, which would otherwise expire after the 2030 tax year.
Where?
Statewide, written into the state constitution at Article XIII, Section 36.
When?
On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the rates never expire. If it fails, the last tax year of the higher rates is 2030.
Why?
The measure’s sponsors, led by the California Teachers Association, frame making the tax permanent as protecting school and children’s healthcare funding from what would otherwise be a revenue loss. Opponents, led by the California Taxpayers Association, argue that Californians already pay among the nation’s highest taxes and that Sacramento should fix its excessive spending before making temporary taxes permanent.
4. Analysis and Assessment
The LAO’s estimate that the Prop 30 income tax surcharge is worth from $5 billion to $15 billion in revenue is effectively a static figure: It assumes that high earners keep living, working, and reporting income in California exactly as they would without the tax. Hoover Institution research examines this assumption directly. Using the full dataset of California tax returns, Hoover Senior Fellow Joshua D. Rauh and coauthor Ryan Shyu studied what happened after Proposition 30 raised top rates in 2012—0.8 percent more of the top-bracket tax base left the state in 2013 than otherwise would have been expected without the tax change. Moreover, the high earners who stayed reported substantially less taxable income; counterintuitively, this was actually the larger effect. Together, these responses erased 45.2 percent of the expected revenue gain in the first year and 60.9 percent of the total gain within the first two years.
A companion Hoover analysis noted that the 2017 federal tax reform which created a cap on state and local tax deductions hit high-income Californians with a force equivalent to 82 percent of another Proposition 30 tax increase. It suggested that the state was likely on the wrong side of the Laffer curve, meaning that increasing the top income tax rates was actually reducing the total tax revenue collected.
Similarly, in an October 2026 op-ed on Proposition 3 itself, Rauh and Hoover fellow Gregory Kearney argue that the top-bracket tax rates are now money losers for California. Before the 2017 cap on state and local tax deductions, high-income Californians could deduct much of their state tax bill on their federal returns. This had the effect of softening the impact of the income tax surcharges. Once the cap took effect, the surcharges imposed by Prop 30 began bearing close to their full weight on the state’s high-income households, which sharpened the incentive to move or restructure income. By the authors’ estimates, since 2018 the state has been losing more tax revenue from departing taxpayers or erosion of the tax base than it collects from those that remain.
Supporters of Prop 3 reply that high earners have not fled California, pointing to studies that find modest migration among millionaires. But Rauh’s earlier findings show why that reply misses the point: Departures accounted for less than a tenth of the lost revenue. Most of the erosion came from taxpayers who stayed and reported less income. This could have occurred by realizing fewer capital gains, shifting business activity to other taxing jurisdictions, or simply working less (or perhaps accepting other forms of income). Effectively, Prop 30 has provided a textbook example of how a tax base can shrink without anyone moving away.
Proposition 3 would also enshrine a revenue structure that Hoover research identifies as a major source of California’s fiscal instability. Hoover Senior Fellow Lee E. Ohanian shows that the top 1 percent of California households now provides roughly 40 to 50 percent of all personal income tax revenue and that the top 10 percent pay almost 90 percent. Because high-earning households tend to receive a large portion of their income from the stock market, which is highly variable, California’s personal income tax revenue surged by 55 percent in 2021 and then fell nearly 35 percent in 2023.
This feast-or-famine paradigm creates complications for funding ongoing programs and exposes California to revenue risk that it has little control over. Rauh and coauthor Jillian Ludwig describe this fragility as “baked into the system” and recommend steering more capital gains revenue into reserves rather than ongoing spending. Proposition 3 does the opposite: It treats the most volatile revenue in the state as a permanent foundation for ongoing commitments.
Moreover, the phrase “the top 2 percent of tax filers” somewhat misrepresents who pays the Prop 30 income tax surcharges. This is because those who pay the tax are not solely a group of consistent high earners. Some Californians would cross the relevant tax threshold only in the year they sell a home they have owned for decades or a small business they built. Capital gains from home sales are taxable when they exceed the home-sale exclusion of $250,000 for single filers and $500,000 for joint filers. Citing a 2025 Redfin analysis, Rauh and Kearney note that 62 percent of California homes have appreciated at least $250,000 in value over their last sale price, and 33 percent had appreciated by at least $500,000. This suggests that a sizable share of California homeowners would see large one-time gains that could push them into the surcharge brackets in the year they sell. Owners of pass-through businesses, who report business profits on their personal returns, would also face these surcharges in successful years or years where they sell their businesses.
The biggest argument made in favor of Proposition 3 is premised on public schools not losing existing funding. However, Hoover research raises the question of where the increased funding has actually gone. By Rauh and Kearney’s calculations, the annual pension contributions for California’s K–12 school districts almost tripled between 2015 and 2023 to about $13 billion (excluding teachers’ own contributions). Over that period, the share of school employee spending devoted to pensions nearly doubled, from about 7 percent to more than 13 percent. If school districts had held pension costs at their 2015 share, Rauh and Kearney estimate, nearly $6 billion more would have been available for other education priorities last year alone. In other words, Prop 30’s income tax surcharges appear to a large extent to be funding increased retirement benefits.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 3 would turn a tax that voters were told was temporary into a permanent feature of the California Constitution. Compared with current law, it raises taxes on high earners from 2031 onward. Hoover Institution research suggests the revenue it protects is considerably smaller than the official estimate because the state’s most mobile taxpayers respond to higher rates by leaving or by reporting less income. It would also lock in California’s reliance on a narrow and volatile tax base while doing nothing to address the pension costs that have absorbed much of the money raised in the name of schools.
Learn More About California
Rather than telling voters what to think, California Decides equips them with the facts, historical context, competing perspectives, and policy implications they need to make informed decisions. Through plain-language explainers, short videos, podcasts, webinars, proposition guides, data visualizations, and expert analysis, the initiative transforms complex public policy into accessible, engaging content for a broad audience.

I'm looking at the Hoover piece, which is strongly opinionated and comes from a conservative-leaning think tank. Its main claim is that Prop 30 erased a large share of the expected tax gain, around 45% in the first year and 61% within two years, citing a Rauh and Shyu study. I want to check that study's details before relying on those numbers.

I'm going to check the other claims in the piece too: the Rauh and Kearney op-ed about the state losing more revenue than it collects, the claim that the Prop 30 money is only about 40% new school funding, the pension cost figures, and the top-earner shares of income tax revenue.

I'm noting the SALT cap as the next effect to check, then re-reading the Hoover line that the measure raises taxes on affected earners going forward, which holds up against current law. The LAO's analysis says about 40 percent of the funding goes to schools and community colleges, with the rest to other state programs and reserves. The supporting case is that the measure keeps rates from expiring rather than raising them now, and the ballot label does call it a tax increase.

I'm now listing the remaining checks: polling from PPIC and Berkeley IGS, the major newspaper endorsements, where the governor candidates stand, and who is funding the yes and no campaigns, including whether any tech billionaires are involved. The governor-race positions seem relevant but probably won't settle the question.

I'm now checking the budget picture: the LAO's November 2025 outlook projected a deficit of about $18 billion for 2026-27 and structural shortfalls of around $35 billion a year after that. I still need to confirm where the enacted 2026-27 budget actually landed. I also want to test the Prop 98 argument, since the LAO's point that the revenue counts toward the school guarantee would mean only part of it is new school money.

I'm weighing whether the revenue loss would actually hit school funding in full. Under the Prop 98 guarantee, only about 40% of the lost General Fund revenue would reduce the school minimum, though the state could choose to backfill the rest. That makes the Yes side's "billions in cuts" claim look like it may overstate the direct effect.

I'm working out how the Prop 98 minimum would shrink if the revenue disappeared, since the EPA money counts toward the guarantee. Under Test 1, that comes to roughly 40% of the lost revenue, or about $2 to $6 billion for schools, with the remainder falling on other state programs.

I'm working through how the Prop 98 minimum would respond to losing the revenue. Since the EPA money counts toward the guarantee, schools would absorb roughly 40% of the lost amount rather than all of it, which makes the Yes side's school-cut figure look more like an upper bound than a direct effect.

I'm working through how the Prop 98 minimum would move if the EPA revenue disappeared. Since that money counts toward the guarantee, the school floor would drop by about 40% of the lost amount, and I'm checking the arithmetic against the General Fund's own school spending.

I'm working through the Prop 98 arithmetic: if the revenue disappears, the school minimum drops by about 40% of the loss, but the General Fund would have to cover more of what schools receive, so the net hit to school totals is smaller than the full revenue loss.

I'm working through the General Fund side of this: if the EPA revenue is gone, schools would lose about 40% of that amount, but the state would have to put roughly 60% of it back into schools from its own budget. The net drop to total school funding is smaller than the full revenue loss, yet the general budget still takes a hit from that backfill.

I'm now checking whether the school loss really works out to 40% of the revenue, and the numbers keep pointing to a larger hit on the general budget. When schools get less money through the guarantee, the state has to cover more of their spending from its own funds, so the rest of the budget absorbs it. That makes the net effect on non-school programs look bigger than the raw revenue loss.

I'm checking the non-school side of the arithmetic: before the measure is gone, the school total is 40% of revenue, with the EPA's share sitting inside it, so the general budget keeps the other 60%. After losing that revenue, the school total drops by about 40% of the loss, but the General Fund has to cover a larger share of schools' spending, so the money left for other programs falls by about $6 billion rather than the full $16 billion I first got.

I'm checking whether the 40% school share still holds under Tests 2 and 3, since the Prop 98 split can shift in other years. The LAO's rough 40% figure fits Test 1, which has been the operative test for most years, so the school loss from the measure could look different in others.

Now I'm weighing the Yes campaign's claims against the LAO analysis. The school share is about 40 percent, so the "billions in cuts" line holds only in part, and the "frees up money for Medi-Cal" line matches the LAO's point about the other 60 percent. I also want to test whether the "money goes straight to the classroom" wording survives, since the revenue counts toward the Prop 98 guarantee and the state could lower its other school spending by the same amount.

I'm checking the Yes side's claim that Prop 3 can't be used for administration, which holds for the EPA money, and the claim that Sacramento can't spend a dollar on bureaucracy, which also holds for that money. I'm also weighing the No side's "largest permanent income tax increase" line, which seems to exaggerate given that the LAO puts the cost at $5 to $15 billion and the comparison is against expiring taxes.

I'm checking whether California's sales tax really is the highest, and it looks like it isn't: states like Tennessee and Louisiana have higher combined rates, though the state-level rate here is among the top. The gas tax claim holds up, and the top income tax rate of 13.3% does appear to be the nation's highest.

I'm now weighing the LAO's view that the measure would extend an income tax on high earners that would otherwise expire in 2031, which makes the Yes side's "not a new tax" framing accurate on paper but misleading in effect. I'm also noting that the $5 to $15 billion cost estimate is a static one, which may overstate the revenue impact if high earners change their behavior.

I'm weighing the fiscal side of the measure: the LAO's $5 to $15 billion estimate may be static, which could overstate the cost if high earners change their behavior. I'm checking whether any independent analysts, such as PPIC or academic economists, have addressed that behavioral response, and whether the budget's structural deficits and reliance on volatile capital gains change the picture.

I'm weighing whether the claimed pension and per-pupil spending effects would actually reduce what reaches classrooms, since EPA money is general-purpose and mixes with other district funds even though it can't pay for administrators.

I'm weighing whether to give a firm yes or no, and the case for yes rests on the $5–15 billion a year the measure would keep flowing, roughly 60% of which lands in general-fund programs like Medi-Cal and reserves. I'm also considering that constitutional protection could shield school funding from being raided in a deficit year.

I'm weighing the case against the measure now: it would make the tax permanent and lock a capital-gains-dependent revenue source into the constitution, and about 60% of the money would free up general fund spending rather than go straight to schools.

I'm weighing whether to give a firm yes or no, and I'm running through the three things that decide it: whether the budget really needs the revenue, whether that revenue would hold up year to year, and whether locking the tax into the constitution is a good idea. I'll give my honest read but make clear this comes down to a values call.

I'm weighing whether the revenue would actually shrink the structural deficit, since losing $5–15 billion could push the state toward cuts or other tax increases, which makes the fiscal case for yes stronger. I'm also noting that failing the measure wouldn't rule out a future tax increase, though that would take a new legislative vote or initiative.

I'm weighing the constitutional lock: it would make the rates hard for the legislature to cut, which opponents see as lost flexibility and supporters see as protection against raiding school funds. I'm also thinking about whether a vote-of-the-people requirement changes the picture compared with a simple two-thirds statute, and I'll need to settle whether to answer yes or no with a brief caveat that it turns on values.

I'm checking the LAO's own figures on the 2012 Prop 30 revenue, which came in at roughly $6 billion a year, and whether actual collections ran above or below projections in the years after. I'm also looking at whether the 2023 drop in income tax receipts, tied to stock market declines, shows how much behavioral response and capital-gains swings matter.

I'm checking how much the revenue shifts in practice, and the Hoover figure of 0.8% of the top-bracket base leaving in 2013 looks modest, though the income-reporting response could make the revenue effect larger. I'm also noting the LAO's roughly 40% share for schools, which is the key nuance behind the Yes side's "billions for schools" framing, and I want to pin down the state budget deficit and LAO projections for the 2026-27 year and see how Prop 40 might interact with this measure.

I'm checking whether Proposition 40, the billionaire wealth tax, also changes income tax rates, since Proposition 3's conflicting-measures clause would apply if it did. A wealth tax may not count as a personal income tax, so I'll need to read its text to see whether the clause is actually triggered.

I'm checking whether the other tax measures on the ballot could interact with Prop 3, since a conflicting-measures clause could matter if one of them also changes personal income tax rates. After that I want to see how the major newspaper editorial boards and the parties have lined up on it.

I'm checking the campaign finance picture, since the Yes side's backers include unions that stand to gain from school funding, though that bears on motives rather than the merits. I'm also verifying the measure's audit and public-accounting claims against its text, and I'll confirm the income tax rate brackets against the LAO's figures.

I'm checking whether the state's fiscal picture would make losing $5–15 billion a year force cuts, and I'm recalling the LAO's late-2025 outlook, which projected a sizable deficit for 2026-27 and structural shortfalls after that. The No side's claim about a surplus turning into a deficit in just three years is the other piece I want to test against the official numbers.

I'm checking the LAO's latest fiscal outlook and any 2026 May Revision updates to see how big the deficit really is and whether losing this revenue would force cuts. I also want to trace the Hoover paper's "60.9%" claim back to its source and see whether it has been peer-reviewed or challenged.

I'm now going through the campaign finance side and the Yes side's union backers, and I'm checking the official Yes and No endorsements from the Democratic and Republican parties. I'll also look at the editorial board positions and the Ballotpedia summary of the campaign.

content.thinking:
I've got a lot of new facts now: about $81 million in reported contributions to Prop 3, which I still need to split between the Yes and No sides. The latest PPIC poll has it at 58% yes and 40% no, with the earlier September and April readings in a similar range, and a sharp partisan divide with most Democrats for it and most Republicans against.

Now I'm comparing how the poll numbers split by age and income, and I'm checking two different reports of the Democratic and Republican breakdown. I'm also noting that the CalMatters piece reports a separate poll figure for a different measure and doesn't bear on this one.

I'm checking the CalMatters income thresholds against the official figures: they list $360,000 and $721,000, while the voter guide has $371,000 and $742,000, which probably reflects a different year's inflation adjustment. I'll go with the official numbers. I'm also noting that Prop 40 is the one-time billionaire tax, Props 41 and 42 are business-backed counter-measures, and Prop 43 would require a two-thirds vote for local taxes.

I'm going to check whether Prop 41 or 42 changes personal income tax rates, since that could bring Prop 3's conflicting-measures clause into play. I also want the total campaign money behind Prop 3 and the full PPIC October report, then the neutral explainers and the Ballotpedia page.

Proposition 3
Make income taxes on higher earners permanent to fund education and healthcare
The tax, first enacted in 2012, is set to expire in 2031. Under the measure, income taxes for top earners range from 10.3% (for individual income over $360,000) to 12.3% (for individual income over $721,000), with graduated rates in between. Eighty-nine percent of the money goes to K-12 public schools and 11% goes to community colleges, with any excess going to public healthcare. The tax typically raises $5 billion to $15 billion a year — about 3% to 10% of overall K-12 spending. The California Teachers Association put this measure on the ballot.

Key Findings
Mail ballots have been sent to all California voters and the November 3 general election is in its final days. Californians are being asked to choose their next governor as well as other state constitutional officers and state legislators; they are also making important policy decisions through 14 state propositions. In addition, the 2026 California midterm ballot features 52 US House races; with a closely divided Congress, a few of these races may help to determine which party controls the 120th Congress. The economy is top of mind, with recent trends in inflation, consumer spending, interest rates, and jobs sending mixed signals.
These are the key findings of the Californians and their Government survey—which includes questions on topics including the November governor’s race, House races, five legislative ballot measures, nine citizens’ initiatives, state issues, and national issues—that was conducted from October 16–October 22, 2026:
Xavier Becerra (D) leads Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) in the governor’s race. Democratic candidates lead Republican candidates in local House district races by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Overwhelming majorities of partisans support their party’s candidates while independents favor the Democratic candidates. Sixty percent are satisfied with the choice of gubernatorial candidates. Sixty-six percent are closely following news about the governor’s race. Fifty-eight percent are more enthusiastic about voting than usual for Congress this year. Majorities say that they would vote yes on Proposition 1 (60%; Housing Bond) and Proposition 2 (61%; Rainy Day Fund), with partisans varying in support; three legislative ballot measures falls short of a majority.
Forty-six percent would vote yes on Proposition 40 (Imposes One-Time Tax) after reading the ballot title and label. Majorities would vote yes on Proposition 3 (58%; Extending Tax on High Incomes), Proposition 37 (65%; Loan Program for Middle-Income Home Buyers), Proposition 38 (57%; Immunology Bond), and Proposition 42 (51%; Prohibits New State Property Taxes). Support varies across partisan groups, and support for five citizens’ initiatives fall short of a majority. Most say the state’s voter information guide is at least “somewhat” useful in deciding how to vote on citizens’ initiatives and report that they are at least “somewhat” satisfied with the information about the citizens’ initiatives.
Half of Californians choose cost of living, inflation, and the economy as well as housing costs and availability as the most important issues facing California today. Majorities of adults and likely voters think the state is headed in the wrong direction, and overwhelming majorities expect the state to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Forty-seven percent of adults and 49 percent of likely voters say they approve of Governor Gavin Newsom’s job performance. Majorities of adults and likely voters say their incomes are not keeping up with inflation and that housing affordability is a big problem in their part of California. Sixty-three percent of likely voters have a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California.
Almost half of Californians name economic conditions and threats to democratic values and norms as the most important problems facing the nation today. Overwhelming majorities of adults and likely voters think the nation is generally going in the wrong direction and expect the nation to have bad times financially in the next 12 months. Twenty-one percent of adults and 26 percent of likely voters say they approve of President Donald Trump’s job performance. About one in four adults and likely voters approve of the job that US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is doing, and a similar share approve of US military action against Iran. About three in ten are very satisfied or somewhat satisfied with the way US democracy is working. Sixty-five percent of likely voters are very confident or somewhat confident that the votes for Congress across the country will be accurately cast and counted in this year’s election.
November Races and Legislative Ballot Measures
Ballots and voter guides for the November 3 election have been mailed to California’s registered voters. At the top of the ticket is the governor’s race, with voters deciding who will replace Gavin Newsom. The 52 House races in California will help to determine the party in control of a closely divided US Congress. Voters will be the deciders on 14 state propositions—five legislative ballot measures and nine citizens’ initiatives—including several tax proposals, multibillion-dollar bonds, and election reforms. Voter engagement is a crucial factor in turnout for this midterm election.
Gubernatorial Election. California likely voters say they would choose Xavier Becerra (D) over Steve Hilton (R) by a 24 point margin (61% to 37%) if the November 3 election for governor were held today. Becerra led Hilton by 22 points in our September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (60% to 38%) and by 25 points in our July survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (61% to 36%). Today, partisans overwhelmingly support their party’s gubernatorial candidate: 92 percent of Democrats support Becerra, and 89 percent of Republicans favor Hilton. Most independent likely voters favor the Democratic candidate for governor (54% Becerra, 41% Hilton), and half or more of likely voters favor Becerra over Hilton across demographic groups and the state’s major regions.
Sixty percent of likely voters say that they are satisfied with their choices of gubernatorial candidates in the November 3 election, while 39 percent are not satisfied. Shares expressing satisfaction with the gubernatorial candidate choices were similar before the June primary (62% May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/)), the 2022 general election (62% October 2022 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) ) , and the 2018 general election (60% October 2018 survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2018/)). Today, majorities of Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) are satisfied, compared to fewer than half of independents (44%). Majorities of Becerra supporters (63%) and Hilton supporters (59%) are satisfied with the gubernatorial candidate choices. Half or more across demographic groups and the state’s major regions are satisfied; notably, satisfaction varies by age (50% 18 to 34; 52% 35 to 54; 69% 55 and older).
About two in three likely voters are closely following news about candidates for the governor’s election (22% very, 44% fairly). In our May survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) before the June primary, about seven in ten were closely following news about candidates in the governor’s election (23% very, 48% fairly). By comparison, about six in ten were closely following news about the candidates in the gubernatorial election in October 2022 (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2022/) (25% very, 35% fairly) and in October 2018 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1018.pdf) (21% very, 41% fairly). Today, majorities across partisan groups (69% Democrats, 70% Republicans, 55% independents) as well as majorities of Becerra and Hilton supporters (65% to 69%) are following news about the gubernatorial candidates at least fairly closely.
House Races. When asked about US House races, likely voters say they would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate by a 28 point margin (63% to 35%). Likely voter preferences were similar in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican), July (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-the-environment-july-2026/) (63% Democrat, 35% Republican), May (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) (64% Democrat, 35% Republican), and February (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-february-2026/) (62% Democrat, 36% Republican). Today, nine in ten or more Democratic and Republican likely voters would choose their party’s House candidate, while most independent likely voters would vote for the Democratic candidate over the Republican candidate (58% to 37%). Majorities across demographic groups and major regions say they would vote for the Democratic candidate in their House district race, with the exception of those in the Inland Empire (47%).
With national attention focused on the 2026 midterms, 58 percent of California likely voters say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections (40% less enthusiastic). About half or more across demographic groups say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual, but there is an “enthusiasm gap” across partisan groups (71% Democrats, 46% Republicans, 46% independents) and between those who would vote for the Democratic (69%) and the Republican (41%) House candidate. Sixty-one percent of likely voters were more enthusiastic about voting for Congress in May, (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-may-2026/) shortly before the June primary, and 52 percent were more enthusiastic in September 2024 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-0924.pdf), ahead of the last congressional election. Today, about half or more across demographic groups and major state regions say they are more enthusiastic about voting than usual in the congressional elections.
Legislative Ballot Measures. We are also tracking support for five propositions that the state legislature placed on the November 3 ballot. Respondents read the full ballot titles and labels.
Proposition 1 (Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs). Sixty percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative statute, which authorizes $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing affordability programs; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 55 percent said they would vote yes and 43 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 1 varies across partisan groups (81% Democrats, 29% Republicans, 54% independents) and between homeowners and renters (54% to 77%). Majorities across demographic groups and the state’s major regions would vote yes on Proposition 1.
Proposition 2 (Increases Rainy Day Fund). Sixty-one percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which increases the rainy day fund approved by voters in 2014; 38 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 60 percent said they would vote yes and 39 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 2 varies across partisan groups (85% Democrats, 23% Republicans, 57% independents). Half or more would vote yes across the state’s major regions and age, gender, education, homeownership, income, and racial/ethnic groups.
Proposition 4 (Repeals Prohibition Against Public Funding of Election Campaigns) . Forty-five percent of likely voters would vote yes on this legislative statute, which repeals a prohibition on state and local governments offering public funding of candidate election campaigns; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 42 percent would vote yes and 53 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 4 varies across partisan groups (60% Democrats, 22% Republicans, 42% independents) and declines with age, income, and homeownership. Support falls short of a majority across regions except in the San Francisco Bay Area (51%).
Proposition 5 (Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers). Forty-five percent of likely voters say they would vote yes on this legislative constitutional amendment, which requires that recall vacancies be filled by subsequent special elections or appointments; 52 percent would vote no. In the September survey (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/), 35 percent said they would vote yes and 59 percent would vote no. Today, support for Proposition 5 differs across partisan groups (56% Democrats, 28% Republicans, 40% independents) and is below 50 percent across regions, with the exception of Los Angeles (50%).
Proposition 43 (Limits Voters’ Ability to Raise Revenues for Local Government Services) . content.thinking:
I'm pulling together the campaign finance figures for the Yes side and the No side. The Yes committees have raised about $81 million, most of it from one education and labor committee, while the No side's main committee shows only around $5,500. That gap in money is striking, though I don't think it settles the question on its own.

The Yes side's committees are the ones with the big totals, while the No side has barely any committee money. I'm weighing that imbalance against the rest, including whether outside spending or other messaging channels could be filling the gap that the committee filings don't show. Endorsements and polling are next, with the partisan splits and the small wording discrepancy about Democratic support to sort out.

I'm checking the rest of the PPIC report for the Prop 3 breakdown, since the press release may not give the reasons behind the numbers. Next I want to verify the claims about behavioral responses to the earlier tax, the budget outlook, and how the editorial boards argued their positions.

I'm going to check whether Prop 41 or Prop 42 touch personal income tax rates, since that decides if the conflict clause in Prop 3 could come into play alongside the billionaire tax in Prop 40. Prop 40 looks like a wealth tax, so it may not qualify, but I want to confirm the wording of each before drawing a conclusion.

I'm going to check whether Prop 40 includes any language about running alongside Prop 3, since some billionaires backing Prop 3 as an alternative to the wealth tax makes that worth confirming. I also want to pull the state budget picture for 2026-27 from the LAO outlook and the enacted budget, and see how Prop 2's rainy day fund measure fits in.

I'm moving on to whether California's per-pupil spending has actually improved relative to other states and whether the extra revenue shows up in outcomes, checking the Yes side's claim against a neutral ranking. I also want to confirm that the top 2% pay about half of state income taxes, and look at how volatile the revenue is given its reliance on capital gains. Last, I'm searching for critiques of the Rauh and Kearney op-ed's claim that the state is losing more revenue from departing taxpayers than it gains.

I'm lining up the research to check next: the Prop 30 behavioral-response evidence, the Rauh and Kearney op-ed, the LAO and enacted 2026-27 budget picture, and the editorial arguments from both the Yes and No endorsers. I also want to see whether the LAO's earlier Prop 30 retrospective shows revenue above projections, since the "45% erosion" figure is contested.

content.text: The Secretary of State's contribution data is striking: about $81 million in reported support against $5,500 in opposition. Next I'll read the editorial boards on both sides, which typically lay out the strongest reasoning, along with the current budget outlook.

Endorsement: Billionaire tax is getting the attention. But Prop 3 will decide California’s future
Prop 3 would make permanent the temporary higher tax rates that voters previously approved to shore up California’s general fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, health care and other programs.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 22, 2026
California’s one-time billionaire tax is getting all the press this election cycle. But there’s another proposed tax on the wealthy this November whose fate is far more essential to the state’s finances: Proposition 3 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf).
The measure doesn’t create a new tax or change existing ones. Instead, it cements high income tax rates on California’s biggest earners.
Those higher rates, which voters first approved in 2012 with Proposition 30 (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2012/30_11_2012.aspx), were supposed to be temporary.
Prop 30 helped California survive the 2008 Great Recession by creating three new tax brackets — with a top marginal rate of 12.3% for the state’s biggest earners. (Those making more than $1 million are also taxed an additional 1%, due to a 2004 voter-approved measure to raise money for mental health services (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2004/63_11_2004.htm).)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 30 raised billions each year for the California budget’s General Fund — the state’s main pot of money for schools, healthcare and other programs.
In 2016, as Prop 30’s temporary rates were set to expire, a coalition of teachers’ unions, state employee unions and healthcare advocacy groups placed Prop 55 on the ballot to keep the rates alive (https://www.lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=55&year=2016). That effort passed.
But the progressive brackets are set to expire once more in 2030. Prop 3 would make them permanent.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how it would work:
Single filers making between $73,000 and $371,000 and joint filers making between $145,000 and $743,000 currently pay (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) a personal income tax rate of 9.3%. Single filers making up to $446,000 and joint filers making up to $892,000 pay an income tax rate of 10.3%. The rate jumps to 11.3% for single filers making up to $743,000 and joint filers making up to $1.5 million. Anyone who makes more pays the max rate of 12.3%.
If voters reject Prop 3, the income tax rate would revert to 9.3% for single filers making over $73,000 and joint filers making more than $145,000. (Those earning more than $1 million would still be taxed an additional 1% from the 2004 measure.)
The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimated (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf) that preserving the current structure would raise between $5 billion and $15 billion annually for the General Fund. Under state spending rules, about 40% of that money would be earmarked for kindergarten through 12th-grade schools and to community colleges. The rest would be divided through the annual budget process — with a large chunk likely going to Medi-Cal, the state’s health insurance program for low-income residents, and some going to reserves.
Obviously, the impact of this measure failing would be enormous.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
With schools still working to recover from the pandemic and the healthcare system facing significant federal cuts under President Donald Trump, rejecting Prop 3 would be a “massive cut … at a time that we are facing massive cuts,” Jodi Hicks, CEO of Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, told the editorial board.
“These revenues are not only essential to schools, but they really are now a fundamental building block of the state budget,” Karen Getman, counsel for the California Teachers Association, told us.
John Kabateck, California director of the National Federation of Independent Business, which opposes Prop 3, countered that the measure would entrench a problematic burden on small businesses. Owners who structure their businesses as “pass-throughs” (https://taxfoundation.org/blog/pass-through-businesses/) pay income taxes rather than corporate taxes — and are thus subject to the increased rates.
“Rejecting Prop 3 would be a welcome sign, frankly, for small businesses,” Kabateck told the editorial board. “Many are still crawling out of the pandemic.”
Of course, that’s also the argument that supporters of Prop 3 make.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
So, where should voters land?
In 2016, the Chronicle’s editorial board encouraged voters not to support Prop 55 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/Chronicle-recommends-No-on-state-Prop-55-9211163.php).
The reasoning was not that California schools and healthcare systems don’t deserve robust funding. It was that Prop 55 was a patch on a much larger problem.
California income tax revenues are inherently volatile. About half come from the top 2% of taxpayers, and therefore tend to fluctuate with the whims of the stock market.
Tying an oversized income tax to a priority as fundamental as public education is reckless. When the market tanks, as it is bound to every few years, California kids take the hardest hit.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
In encouraging voters to reject Prop 55, this editorial board’s hope was that it would force state leaders to do the hard work of comprehensively reforming California’s tax system to reduce boom-and-bust cycles and instead permit stable, sustainable investment in schools, healthcare and other priorities.
That didn’t happen.
Instead, we’re getting more patches — from Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax, to Gov. Gavin Newsom and state lawmakers’ absurd decisions to raise taxes on healthcare and everyday software products (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/article/tax-money-state-california-22325976.php).
It’s true that voters in 2020 rejected a measure (https://calmatters.org/education/2020/11/prop-15-defeat-california-schools/) that would have modified Prop 13, the infamous 1978 measure that capped property taxes, by permitting higher taxes on large commercial properties.
With Prop 13 seemingly untouchable, income tax “seems to be the way that the voters are comfortable going” to increase revenue, Getman said.
But split roll wasn’t a solution for Prop 13, either. Voters understood that California can’t solve its issues by simply layering more taxes on top of a system that is inherently flawed.
California has the most regressive state sales taxes in the nation and an absurd income tax that hits someone making $73,000 the same as someone who makes $371,000. Even David Gamage, one of the authors of the billionaire tax, told the editorial board that he was “uncomfortable” with a top marginal income tax rate of 13.3%.
California’s tax system needs wholesale reform — by collecting stable revenue from those who can afford it and giving tax relief to the struggling middle class.
We also need greater accountability. California’s per-student spending has skyrocketed in recent years, yet academic outcomes haven’t improved commensurately (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-housing-education-reading-literacy-20288858.php). Our politicians use budget windfalls to create new programs they know they won’t be able to fund in bad times (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2025/03/health-care-california-budget-deficit/) — and then pass flawed patches to make up the difference.

Prop 3 won’t resolve these problems.
And yet, in the wake of the pandemic and amid a dystopian federal climate under Trump, California also can’t afford to further reduce ongoing funds — unstable as they may be — for schools and healthcare programs. Voters should support Prop 3 to sustain funding levels but keep pressure on their politicians to work toward a fairer and more sustainable tax system. Because the one we have can and will fail.

Endorsement: No on Proposition 3, ‘temporary’ taxes should be temporary

By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 2, 2026 at 4:23 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
Temporary should mean temporary. But for the government, temporary often means forever.
That’s what’s happening with Proposition 3 on the Nov. 3 ballot, titled: “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Healthcare by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes,” which, as the name suggests, seeks to lock in the state’s high income tax rates forever.
The story goes back to 2012, with Proposition 30, which imposed both a statewide sales tax increase through 2016 and an increase to top income tax rates through 2018.
Leading the push for Prop. 30 was Gov. Jerry Brown, who vowed it was only a temporary measure to help the state ride out tough budget times in the years after the Great Recession and ensure the state’s schools were reliably funded. In fact, Prop. 30 was titled, “Temporary Taxes to Fund Education.” Taken together with other voter-approved income taxes, this pushed top income tax rates to 13.3%, the highest in the nation according to the Tax Foundation, with Hawaii the runner-up at 11%.
It wasn’t long before the state’s public employee unions pounced to extend the “temporarily” increased top income tax rates over the objections of even Gov. Brown. In 2016, voters approved the extension with Proposition 55, with the taxes set to run through 2030 and expiring in 2031. As this editorial board warned at the time in opposing Prop. 55, “California will not be able to tax its way to prosperity, and imposing more taxes, particularly on those most capable of making investments here (and most capable of leaving or shifting their investments to more business-friendly states) will only reduce job opportunities and suppress economic growth.”
The argument in favor of Prop. 3 seen by voters argues that allowing Prop. 55 to expire “would give millionaires and billionaires a massive tax cut at the expense of our classrooms, clinics and communities.” But that assumes the wealthy producers will stay here, instead of getting an instant tax cut by moving to Texas or elsewhere, especially when considered in an environment in which wealth taxes are seriously being talked about.
Indeed, research published by the American Economic Association in 2024 by Joshua Rauh and Ryan J. Shyu found that the Prop. 30 tax hikes prompted many high-income earners to either leave California or lower their taxable income. Such “responses eroded 45.2 percent of state windfall tax revenues within the first year and 60.9 percent within 2 years, driven largely by the intensive margin,” Rauh and Shyu reported.

Beyond the perils of maintaining such a high tax environment, the reality is that high taxes have primarily served to paper over the fundamental budget problems of the state and the education system. As Rauh recently noted, “In California, over the 9 most recent years of data, contributions to pensions for K-12 nearly doubled as a share of educational budgets, and consumed 44% of the increase in school budgets. Prop 30/55 looks more like a tax to fund pensions than a tax to fund education.”
That’s the cold, hard reality behind any public proclamation that higher taxes are needed to help students.
Also, to reiterate, the existing Prop. 55 tax rates run through 2030, expiring in 2031. That gives Californians plenty of time, including election cycles in 2028 and 2030, to decide whether the state truly needs another extension of our sky-high income tax rates. There’s no urgent need for an extension in 2026, let alone to make the “temporary” tax hikes permanent.
R obbing future voters of their decision-making because the California Teachers Association wants to secure a revenue stream years ahead of time is unjustified.
Vote no on Prop. 3.

By U T Editorial Board (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/author/u-t-editorial-board/)
PUBLISHED: September 18, 2026 at 5:30 PM PDT
Getting your Trinity Audio (https://trinityaudio.ai/) player ready...
One of the most enduring canards in public policy debates is the claim that school quality is a function of school spending. In California, this is easily disproven. Adjusted for inflation, the state spends far more per K-12 pupil now than it did in 2006-07, per (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5087) the Legislative Analyst’s Office. It’s now at an all-time high of $27,418 per student (https://www.hatchingresults.com/blog/californias-2026-27-budget).
But even as students in the Golden State are far more likely to get straight As (https://nypost.com/2026/09/13/us-news/california-high-school-gpas-soar-as-college-math-skills-decline/) than ever, their test scores have been mediocre or worse (https://www.ppic.org/publication/californias-k-12-test-scores/) for decades. Both red states that spend much less per-pupil (Mississippi) and blue states that spend somewhat more (Massachusetts) do significantly better jobs of preparing their high school graduates for college and life in general, according to (https://nces.ed.gov/nationsreportcard/) National Assessment of Educational Progress data.
This history is why the U-T Editorial Board has long argued that K-12 funding in the Golden State needs to be linked to the adoption of basic reforms of the sort embraced by Massachusetts in 1993 and Mississippi in 2013 — reforms that emphasized improved teaching as crucial to improved student performance. The most successful Democratic presidents of the past 50 years — Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — considered it common sense to coach up struggling teachers as well as struggling students.
This history is why we oppose Proposition 3 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026), placed on the ballot directly by the Legislature. It would make permanent what was first sold to voters in 2012 as a “temporary” surcharge on income taxes of wealthy residents to keep K-12 funding at adequate levels. That’s still the pitch in 2026. “Protect Local Schools Without Raising Taxes,” reads the headline on the Yes on Prop. 3 website (https://www.yesprop3ca.com/?gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=24261092554&gbraid=0AAAABEpNOQuVbaqhqGUD_FcE0tO11_EO0&gclid=CjwKCAjwwrPVBhA1EiwAv_YO-R7oAdCydz_5z0MiP0qdoGtMtcAnfk1sBvOKXl8xJj30PLr576PWPBoCmIwQAvD_BwE) — “Proposition 3 keeps the current tax rates on the wealthiest top 2% with strict accountability to ensure every dollar gets to classrooms, not Sacramento politicians.”
But “strict accountability” is not a term a rational person would associate with California’s public schools. As Stanford researchers documented (https://scale.stanford.edu/sites/default/files/GDTFII_Report_Henig.pdf), the Obama administration’s Race to the Top (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Race_to_the_Top) initiative that offered increased federal funding to districts that adopted reforms went nowhere in our state because of the program’s accountability edicts.
Teachers have a difficult job, and most are hardworking and eager to help their students. But in California, the unions that represent them depict attempts to measure their effectiveness as corporate attacks (https://rethinkingschools.org/articles/from-the-race-to-the-top-to-the-plunge-to-the-bottom/) on public education. In doing so, they show they value the interests of school employees over the interests of students — and society in general. Vote no on Proposition 3 to send the message that this is wrong.

I'm going through the editorial board arguments now. The SF Chronicle backs the measure, noting it doesn't add a new tax and simply locks in current rates, with about 40% of the revenue going to schools. Its main worry is that tying an oversized income tax to education could be risky if the market drops, and it points out that the paper opposed Prop 55 too.

The OC Register opposes it, arguing that "temporary should mean temporary," and cites a 2024 study finding that states offset most of such windfall revenue within two years. It also notes that K-12 pension contributions have consumed a large share of school budget increases. The SD Union-Tribune's position is next.

I'm moving on to the UT's position: it centers on school outcomes, pointing to record per-pupil spending of $27,418 alongside mediocre test scores, and it calls for teacher-effectiveness reforms and resistance to CTA influence. I'm also noting that its objections are about education policy more than the tax itself. I want to check the Rauh and Shyu citation next, since the attribution to a specific journal is still unclear to me.

I'm working through the numbers now: even after the behavioral erosion, the remaining share of the windfall would still be positive revenue, roughly 40% of the static estimate. I also want to test that against the LAO's $5–15B figure, since a 60% erosion over two years would cut into it substantially, and I'm weighing two caveats about whether the Rauh and Shyu windfall applies to Prop 3 at all.

I'm checking whether the paper's finding that high earners mostly responded by shifting when they realized income, rather than leaving, holds up, since timing effects could mean the erosion isn't permanent. I also want to confirm the LAO's read on Prop 30 revenue against the earlier estimates, and find critiques of the Rauh and Shyu study.

I'm checking the state budget picture next, including the LAO's fiscal outlook and how the No side's claim about a swing from surplus to deficit holds up. I also want to see where the governor stands on Prop 3, since the SF Chronicle piece references recent tax decisions in Sacramento.

Next I want to check the state budget outlook, including whether the current 2026-27 budget already counts on this revenue, since the tax would expire around 2031 and that would open a fiscal hole in the structural deficit.

# Research shows that when California hiked taxes on the rich they left and revenues were only half those forecast
The new issue of the *American Economic Journal: Economic Policy* is out and it contains a study by economists Joshua Rauh and Ryan Shyu titled “Behavioral Responses to State Income Taxation of High Earners: Evidence from California.”
Back in 2019, I wrote about an earlier version of this study that examined “the effects of personal income taxation on household location choice and pre-tax income”:
> In 2012, Californians facing “temporary” multi-billion dollar budget deficits passed Proposition 30.
This included a 3.45% sales tax increase as well as a $42 billion “temporary” increase in the state’s progressive income tax rates.
Rauh and Shyu find that wealthy Californians were about 40% more likely to leave after the income tax hike, mostly to states without income taxes.
They also found that these departures and other responses to increased taxes eliminated 45.2% of the revenue the state expected to get from high earners.
Within two years, 60.9% of this windfall had been eroded.

## Abstract
Drawing on the universe of California income tax filings and the variation imposed by a 2012 tax increase of up to 3 percentage points for high-income households, we present new findings about the effects of personal income taxation on household location choice and pre-tax income.
First, over and above baseline rates of taxpayer departure from California, an additional 0.8% of the California residential tax filing base whose 2012 income would have been in the new top tax bracket moved out from full-year residency of California in 2013, mostly to states with zero income tax.
Second, to identify the impact of the California tax policy shift on the pre-tax earnings of high-income California residents, we use as a control group high-earning out-of-state taxpayers who persistently file as California non-residents.
Using a differences-in-differences strategy paired with propensity score matching, we estimate an intensive margin elasticity of 2013 income with respect to the marginal net-of-tax rate of 2.5 to 3.3.
Among top-bracket California taxpayers, outward migration and behavioral responses by stayers together eroded 45.2% of the windfall tax revenues from the reform.

# Taxes and Migration: New Evidence from Academic Research
In its first issue of 2024, the *American Economic Journal: Economic Policy* published three academic articles addressing a complex relationship between state taxes and individual decisions on where to live and work in the United States.
...
The second article, “Behavioral Responses to State Income Taxation of High Earners: Evidence from California,” by Joshua Rauh and Ryan Shyu, focuses on California’s Proposition 30, which significantly increased marginal tax rates for high-earning individuals in the state in 2012.
The authors use administrative microdata and modern methods of causal analysis to demonstrate that high earners were indeed very sensitive to Proposition 30.
In response to the 3-percentage-point increase in the top marginal state income tax rate, which reached 13.3 percent in 2012, high earners reported $321,000-$436,000 less in taxable income during 2012-2014—about 10 percent of their baseline income of $4.15 million.
The likely reasons were the reduction in labor supply, shifting income-generating activities to other countries, or other forms of tax avoidance.
Rauh and Shyu also discuss the implications of the SALT cap deduction introduced as part of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, arguing that this cap increased the incentives for high-income individuals to consider moving to lower-tax states even more than Proposition 30 did.

California’s richest are doing great.
Over the last four decades, while the bottom four-fifths of households have seen their real incomes decline, the top 1% have seen their real incomes grow two and half times (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/should-voters-approve-prop-3-how-top-tax-rates-have-helped-californians/). This upper stratum now earns in a week what the middle fifth of Californians make in a year.
Proposition 3 asks the Californians truly living the California dream to keep paying their fair share. No more. No less.
Vote for Proposition 3.
